#7611. Setting Guidelines for Using AI in the Classroom

Teachers are doing their best to guide student use of artificial intelligence, but it’s clear that some boundaries are desperately needed.

Stop signs are common. Before the start of this school year, New York City officials banned the use of generative AI for public preschools through eighth grade, and Los Angeles educators banned access to generative AI platforms on school devices for all grade levels.

Parents seem to agree: In recent polls, 75% of them reported supporting pausing AI in schools. But a nearly identical share of respondents (73%) say children already use AI for schoolwork. The technology is here, and let’s face it: Pauses aren’t a long-term solution. Teachers and children need clear guidelines.

AI, after all, is embedded in many online platforms. Alphabet (Google’s parent company) has offered discounted Chromebooks to schools since at least 2011, and Gemini is included in Google’s Chrome web browser. Since Google does not allow its AI summaries or chatbot to be turned off, Fairfax County Public Schools developed its own plug-in to block Google AI search results.

>>> Families and Students Need Guidance on AI

School districts across the country are deciding which forms of AI to ban and for which grade levels, but those choosing to use AI would do well to consider proactive uses of the technology and methods for responsible integration.

State lawmakers must define academic standards and adopt appropriate guardrails for responsible use of AI in classrooms. At its worst, students use AI for companionship in place of friends and to do their homework or write their essays. At its best, students use AI to find, collect, and distill information and identify errors in their own work. AI learning platforms can measure student proficiency in a lesson and build exercises according to their level, following teacher-led instruction.

Even New York City’s restrictions are not banning all forms of AI at the lower grades. City officials allow for the use of programs such as Quill, which helps students with reading comprehension and research and Edia, a math program.

The Heritage Foundation developed model legislation for AI in schools that allows for responsible use of AI in classrooms. The model prioritizes human-centered learning and oversight, transparency, safety and data security. Schools should not be required to adopt AI into lesson plans, but for those that do, educators should help students recognize the difference between getting assistance with homework questions and plagiarism.

State lawmakers should respect parent rights and require schools to obtain parent consent for AI use. Educators should offer parents and students alternatives when families choose to opt out. AI vendors should not gather student data for targeted advertising or sell or rent this information.

Likewise, educators must adhere to state and federal privacy laws such as the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act.

While school officials can allow generative AI programs, teachers should prohibit the use of AI companions that mimic personal relationships. Romantic conversations or simulated friendships do not have academic use and interfere with children’s social skills and healthy development.

>>> The Promise and Peril of Artificial Intelligence in Education  

Florida recently adopted rules for AI in schools that are consistent with many of these provisions. State officials recognize that teachers and students can use AI effectively and banning AI will not eliminate the use of large language models (LLMs) but cause the activity to go unmonitored. If AI use goes underground, the potential for cheating increases, with potentially disastrous consequences for student learning.

Lawmakers should use lessons already available in research and in the media on effective and ineffective uses of technology to advance policy ideas dedicated to protecting student privacy and promoting student learning. Educators can harness the benefits that come from new technologies like AI to help students extend their abilities and not erase them.

State officials should adopt thoughtfully designed boundaries for student and teacher use of AI, including restrictions on non-academic uses of AI. These provisions can allow teachers to blend AI into instructional guidance and help prepare students for the future. AI is part of that future, so let’s use it to our advantage.

#7609. No, Mamdani, Socialism Does Not Increase Affordability

Of the many inane comments that socialists have made this year, the one that democracy is “the building block of socialism” might be the most absurd.

Who made the comment? You guessed it: New York City’s boy genius, Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

In a recent episode of “This Past Weekend,” Mr. Mamdani discussed socialism’s ability to ensure affordability with comedian Theo Von. The interview was replete with Marxian nonsense, but Mr. Mamdani also discussed many Americans’ economic frustrations: homeownership feels out of reach; rent is expensive; childcare is unaffordable; and grocery prices are substantially higher.

Young people increasingly feel that the American dream is “slipping away.”

Recognizing affordability problems, however, is not the same as identifying the causes. Mr. Mamdani avers that the free market system cannot solve these problems and that socialism is the silver bullet.

Consider his assertion about democracy. When Mr. Von brought up the concept, Mr. Mamdani interrupted him and claimed, “That’s the building block of socialism.”

>>> Mamdani’s City Grocery Plan Could Leave Taxpayers Paying for Every Banana

Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels would like to have a word.

To them, it was clear that implementing socialism—a word that they used interchangeably with communism—would require the opposite of democracy: tyranny.

In their 1848 “The Communist Manifesto,” the owner’s manual for Marxism, Marx and Engels rightly predicted that people would fight back when the government seized their property—something Mr. Mamdani should bear in mind as he upsets more and more New Yorkers with property-grabbing schemes.

“The proletariat will use its political supremacy to wrest, by degrees, all capital from the bourgeoisie, to centralize all instruments of production in the hands of the State,” Marx and Engels wrote. “Of course, in the beginning, this cannot be effected except by means of despotic inroads on the rights of property, and on the conditions of bourgeois production.”

So, no, Mr. Mamdani. Socialism’s pillars are totalitarian, based on forced nationalization and coercive state control.

Now, let us deal with the fanciful claim that socialism is the best way to order society: “Socialism to me means that you have whatever you need to live a dignified life, and it’s the government’s job to deliver on that.”

It sounds compassionate, but what happens when the government assumes responsibility for determining, financing and delivering the necessities of a “dignified life”?

Here, we begin to understand why Mr. Mamdani mixes socialism with democracy. To him, democracy is not just about electing leaders; it is also about letting people choose things that they cannot afford, courtesy of taxpayers.

In line with his big-government agenda, he explained socialism as “the extension of democracy from the ballot box to the rest of your life … your workplace, your home.”

Yet socialists devalue real democracy when they define it as the “right” for people to own what they have not earned. They also devalue the protection of inalienable rights when they insist that 51% of the electorate can suppress individual liberties such as property rights—something America’s Founders called “mobocracy.”

A free society empowers majorities, but it also protects individual rights. More government intervention will neither expand liberty nor make New York City more affordable.

The Big Apple is indeed the most expensive city in the United States and the third most expensive in the world. Mr. Mamdani said that is because “greed is baked into a lot of this economy.” He portrays capitalist profit incentives as a motive for firms to exploit workers, reduce the quality of goods and break the law.

Still, profit and wealth are not social defects to be discouraged; quite the contrary. In competitive markets, signals indicate that entrepreneurs have found ways to provide goods and services that consumers value. These incentives encourage businesses to innovate, produce more, reduce costs and discover better ways to meet people’s needs.

This must be a foreign concept to Mr. Mamdani, who believes that it is the government’s duty to provide the public with everything, from rent to groceries. He ignores commonsense solutions that have worked the world over, such as tax cuts and deregulation—and deportations, for that matter, which would reduce costs for households and businesses alike.

>>> Mamdani Is about to Make Housing Even More Expensive

Instead, Mr. Mamdani turns to central planning, even though government bureaucrats created many of the affordability problems he now insists they will solve.

Take housing. Mr. Mamdani argues that housing costs are central to New York’s economic problems, and many economists agree. Yet the city’s affordability crisis results from decades of restrictive zoning, burdensome permit requirements, development constraints, rent regulation and political barriers that limit housing construction.

The pattern is familiar: Government intervention distorts the market, consumers suffer the consequences, then socialists point to those consequences as evidence of market failure requiring still more state intervention.

Throughout his interview with Mr. Von, Mr. Mamdani framed his socialist ideology as empathetic, not the state-controlled subjugation that it is. Yet remember, the more “necessities” the government promises to provide, the more power bureaucrats require to deliver them.

When the government assumes control over housing, childcare, grocery access, transportation and healthcare, citizens become less self-reliant and more dependent on political institutions.

Americans are right to be concerned about affordability, but the challenge facing them today is how to improve markets with more freedom and opportunity, not socialism.

James Thomas Ashbacher, 37, of Spring Lake, North Carolina, a former U.S. government contractor, was arrested by the FBI on Tuesday for allegedly leaking national defense information by posting the information on a popular social media site, unlawfully retaining other national defense information at his residence, and stealing night vision goggles from the U.S. Army’s Special Operations Command.

The classified materials were later re-posted by other users to a second social media site. Ashbacher asked a social media user in a private message to remove some materials and further stated that he was “trying to do some damage control.” A search of Ashbacher’s residence also revealed a classified award write-up that contained additional national defense information, along with a night vision goggle system specific to a military unit within Army Special Operations Command that had been reported missing.

The FBI Charlotte Field Office is investigating the case with substantial assistance from the U.S. Department of the Army’s Criminal Investigative Division.

Trial Attorney Leslie Esbrook of the National Security Division’s Counterintelligence and Export Control Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Logan Liles for the Eastern District of North Carolina are prosecuting the case.

#7606. Court Dismisses Claims Over Alleged "Doxing" and Criticism of Homelessness / Needle Exchange Activists

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From Stabbin Wagon v. City of Medford, decided Sept. 30 by Judge Mustafa Kasubhai (D. Ore.):

The Court assumes the following alleged facts are true. Stabbin' Wagon is a Medford non-profit that provides clean needles, food and aid, and outreach services to unhoused people, particularly those suffering from drug addiction and mental illnesses. Plaintiff Jones was the founder and executive director of Stabbin' Wagon and Plaintiff Strong was an employee. Plaintiffs frequently criticized the City's arrests of unhoused individuals and its failure to provide outreach services to those individuals.

Defendants Brian Sjothun, Randy Sparacino, Justin Ivens, Darrel Graham, Geoff Kirkpatrick, Trevor Arnold, Arturo Vega, and John and Jane Does (collectively, "City Defendants") are current and former Medford city officials and police officers. City Defendants have criticized Plaintiffs and their needle exchange program. Starting around 2021, Defendants Graham, Kirkpatrick, and Sparacino monitored the Plaintiffs' social media activities, protest attendance, and interviews with newspapers. City Defendants removed Plaintiffs from police communications which alerted local outreach services when the police swept an encampment of unhoused individuals. Medford police have also stopped, arrested, and cited Stabbin' Wagon employees on several occasions from 2020 to 2023.

In 2023, Plaintiffs received a $1.5 million grant from the Oregon Health Authority ("OHA") to open a 'respite center' to provide more outreach services to unhoused people. Defendants Sjothun, Ivens, Arnold, and Kirkpatrick attempted to persuade OHA to rescind the grant. Plaintiffs allege that these Defendants "disseminated inflammatory, false, and disparaging information about Plaintiffs to other providers, state officials, and community leaders" in their attempt to reverse the grant.

Defendant Ryan Mallory is "a law-enforcement-adjacent figure in Southern Oregon" who operates social media platforms and companies that investigate, report, and consult on matters related to law enforcement, including the Medford Police Department. Defendant Mallory supported City Defendants' attempt to rescind the grant. He expressed his opposition to Plaintiffs' OHA grant on his Facebook group which has over 100,000 followers. His followers commented in support, and on September 13, 2023, one approached Plaintiffs while they were working and threatened to call the police. On August 4, 2023, Defendant Mallory posted Plaintiffs' personal information, including their home addresses and birthdays, in a graphic with Plaintiffs' likenesses resembling "law enforcement booking records." On September 7, 2023, Defendant Mallory posted a video and a comment that urged the public to oppose the OHA grant, stating in part:

Unqualified people that fill our Parks in greenways with needles, keep people addicted by promoting drug use, and misappropriate grant money by using it for public protest of the police rather than helping people are about to get a massive paycheck …. Ask for an audit of the stabbin wagon organization…. These folks are intending on renting a building to perpetuate drug use …. Melissa Jones and her marketing director [Sam Strong] have openly stated that they get grant money and use it to protest police and others.

Defendant Mallory and his followers continued making posts that "fomented animosity and disinformation regarding Plaintiffs and their services." On May 21, 2024, Defendant Mallory posted an article that discussed Plaintiff Jones's sentencing in municipal court and commented that she "[d]efinitely hasn't learned her lesson based on that. Guess we'll see how probation goes." In March 2025, Defendant Mallory posted a video that showed needles on the ground in downtown Medford and commented that Stabbin' Wagon "shouldn't be in business at all, it worsens the problem."

OHA delayed Plaintiffs' grant but ultimately awarded the funds. "[M]unicipal and zoning barriers and Defendants' subversion campaign" forced Plaintiffs to end their attempt to open the respite center. Plaintiffs Jones and Strong resigned from Stabbin' Wagon due to the Defendants' "harassment, surveillance, doxing, and retaliatory pressure." …

The court dismissed plaintiffs' claims (which related to doxing, criticism, surveillance, and retaliation) on various grounds, including that they were filed too late, but also added this:

Plaintiffs also allege that Defendants retaliated against Plaintiffs advocacy by opposing their grant from OHA and publicly and privately disparaging them. Plaintiffs allege that immediately after OHA awarded Stabbin' Wagon the grant, the City and Medford police, including Defendants Sjothun, Ivens, Arnold, and Kirkpatrick disseminated false and misleading information to state officials, community leaders, and other organizations. Plaintiffs allege the City sought to portray Stabbin' Wagon as extreme and unqualified, lobbied OHA, and coordinated with other nonprofits hostile to Stabbin' Wagon like OnTrack Rogue Valley and the Addictions Recovery Center.

Courts take a cautious approach with retaliation claims involving government speech like those here.

Restricting the ability of government decisionmakers to engage in speech risks interfering with their ability to effectively perform their duties. It also ignores the competing First Amendment rights of the officials themselves. The First Amendment is intended to "preserve an uninhibited marketplace of ideas in which truth will ultimately prevail." That marketplace of ideas is undermined if public officials are prevented from responding to speech of citizens with speech of their own.

The Ninth Circuit has accordingly set a high bar for when government speech gives rise to a First Amendment retaliation claim. For example, an act of defamation does not give rise to a retaliation claim if it does not affect the plaintiff's rights, benefits, or status with the state. Government speech that results in reputational harm and ultimately a loss in employment also does not meet the high bar for adverse action….

False accusations may give rise to a retaliation claim in certain contexts, however. In Mendocino Env't Ctr. v. Mendocino County (9th Cir. 1999), police officers falsely accused members of an environmental organization of criminal activity in connection with a criminal investigation. The officers made false accusations to secure arrest and search warrants. The Ninth Circuit held that plaintiffs sufficiently alleged a First Amendment retaliation claim because the inclusion of the accusations in warrant affidavits permitted the inference that the acts would chill a person of ordinary firmness from future first amendment activities.

At the outset, some of Plaintiffs' allegations fail because they seek to hold Defendants accountable for protected speech. For example, Plaintiffs allege that Defendants Ivens and Arnold "expressed outrage over the award and attempted to mobilize public opposition and influence OHA to rescind the grant." They also allege that the City portrayed "Stabbin' Wagon as untrustworthy, unqualified, and politically extreme." These allegations are insufficient to give rise to Plaintiffs' retaliation claim because the government must be allowed to express its own views, even when it is critical of some of its citizens….

Plaintiffs [also] allege that OHA delayed Stabbin' Wagon's grant in response to Defendants' conduct but ultimately awarded it. Plaintiffs Jones and Strong resigned from Stabbin' Wagon and Plaintiffs had to close their peer respite program. Plaintiffs, however, do not allege that Defendants had any control over the grant process and conceded that point at oral argument. This is fatal to Plaintiffs' allegations that Defendants "disseminated inflammatory, false, and disparaging information about Plaintiffs." Cf. Gini v. Las Vegas Metro. Police Dep't (9th Cir. 1994) (holding defamatory statements did not give rise to a First Amendment violation where the officials "could not, and did not, make any decision or take any state action affecting [the plaintiff's] rights, benefits, relationship or status with the state")….

And the court had this to say about plaintiffs' civil rights conspiracy claim:

A plaintiff bringing a Section 1985 claim to vindicate rights secured by the First Amendment must "prove that the state was somehow involved in or affected by the conspiracy" because the First Amendment "restrains only official conduct." Plaintiffs remaining allegations are that unspecified Defendants coordinated "with anti-activist social media groups that published private information and incited public backlash" and disseminated "Plaintiffs' private identifying information, obtained through law enforcement channels, to more than 100,000 followers in order to incite harassment and vigilantism against Plaintiffs."

Plaintiffs make numerous allegations attributing this conduct to Defendant Mallory who is not a City official. Much of Plaintiffs' allegations center on Defendant Mallory's speech via social media and other outlets. Digital communications like these generally fall within the First Amendment's protections. Speech is generally protected unless it falls into a category of unprotected speech [such as the category of "true threats"]. Some of these allegations seek to impose liability for protected speech and therefore fail. E.g., SAC [Second Amended Comalaint] ¶ 121 (alleging Defendant Mallory criticized Plaintiffs' qualifications). Plaintiffs summarily allege categories of potentially unprotected speech by Defendant Mallory. E.g., SAC ¶¶ 129, 131 (alleging Plaintiffs experienced harassment); SAC (alleging defamatory statements); SAC ¶ 203.e (incitement). To the extent Plaintiffs seek to hold Defendant Mallory liable for these acts, Plaintiffs must identify the alleged unprotected speech with more specificity and without relying on broad legal conclusions.

Plaintiffs also allege Defendant Mallory published Plaintiffs' names and home addresses in a "[b]usted" graphic, mimicking booking log services. A party generally cannot maintain a claim for disclosure of publicly available information that is lawfully obtained. Florida Star v. B.J.F. (1989). Plaintiffs do not allege their names and home addresses were not publicly available or unlawfully obtained. Plaintiffs therefore have not alleged an overt act by Defendant Mallory.

With respect to the City Defendants, Plaintiffs allege that the "City Defendants, in particular the members of the Medford Police Department, were aware of Defendant Mallory's pro-law enforcement social media influence." Plaintiffs further allege that Defendants Kirkpatrick and Sparacino appeared on Defendant Mallory's podcast. Plaintiff makes the general allegation that "Defendants … reached a tacit understanding that Defendant Mallory would" amplify the City Defendants' retaliation against Plaintiffs.

Viewed in light of the Court's rulings above, these allegations are insufficient to allege the participation of the City Defendants in the alleged disclosure of Plaintiffs' personal information. A plaintiff must allege a conspiracy with facts that rise above allegations of parallel conduct and sympathetic viewpoints. Plaintiffs' general allegation of tacit agreement is insufficient. The Court has found that Plaintiffs have not adequately alleged the City Defendants retaliated against them, so Defendant Mallory cannot be said to have amplified it at this time. Plaintiffs' Section 1985(3) claim is dismissed because they must allege that "two or more persons conspire[d]" and that a state actor is "at least one of the wrongdoers." …

Stephanie C. Kucera and Zachariah H. Allen (Hart Wagner LLP) and Casey S. Murdock (Frohnmayer Deatherage Law Firm) represent defendants.

NEXT: Crime in Texas, Trial in Texas, Confession to Clergy in North Carolina: Which Law Applies?

Eugene Volokh is the Thomas M. Siebel Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, and the Gary T. Schwartz Distinguished Professor of Law Emeritus and Distinguished Research Professor at UCLA School of Law. Naturally, his posts here (like the opinions of the other bloggers) are his own, and not endorsed by any institution. He is also the co-host of the Free Speech Unmuted podcast.

#7605. Crime Is Down: Why Leadership Matters

For years, Americans were told by the left that rising crime was either exaggerated, the result of poverty, caused by COVID, or simply the unavoidable cost of modern life. None of those assertions is true.

Victims, police officers, prosecutors, and families living in high-crime neighborhoods knew better. They understood that crime is not an abstraction. It is a stolen vehicle, a broken window, a family traumatized by violence, or a neighborhood slowly surrendered to fear.

That is why the preliminary results of the just-released 2025 National Crime Victimization Survey (NCVS) deserve serious attention. The numbers point in one direction: crime fell substantially across nearly every major category measured by the survey.

The results are preliminary, and responsible observers will await final estimates and additional analysis. But the trend is unmistakable—and it coincides with a national agenda that has placed public safety, border security, law enforcement, and support for victims at the center of federal policy.

According to the preliminary estimates from the Bureau of Justice Statistics, the rate of serious violent victimization—violent crime excluding simple assault—fell 25%, from 9.9 victimizations per 1,000 people age 12 or older in 2024 to 7.4 per 1,000 in 2025. Aggravated assault declined even more sharply, dropping 31% from 4.5 to 3.1 per 1,000.

>>> Americans Lost Over $20 Billion to One Type of Crime. Here’s How We Can Fight It

The property-crime figures are equally striking. Property victimization declined 19%, from 138.0 per 1,000 households to 111.2 per 1,000. Burglary or trespassing fell 25%. Motor vehicle theft declined 30%, representing approximately 349,000 fewer stolen vehicles. Other household theft declined 19%, while burglary and trespassing represented roughly 460,000 fewer victimizations.

These are not minor statistical adjustments. They represent fewer people harmed, fewer families disrupted, and fewer communities forced to absorb the economic and emotional costs of crime.

The NCVS is particularly important because it captures criminal victimization whether or not the victim reported the offense to police. Each year, the Bureau of Justice Statistics gathers information from a nationally representative sample of approximately 240,000 people age 12 or older in about 150,000 households.

It therefore complements the FBI’s Uniform Crime Reporting data, which are based primarily on information supplied by law enforcement agencies.

The two measures tell a consistent story. The FBI’s 2025 data showed the largest year-to-year decline in violent crime since the agency began tracking national crime trends in 1936. Murder and non-negligent manslaughter declined by an estimated 18.1%.

The NCVS now provides an important second measure, reflecting the experiences of victims themselves.

What explains the decline? No serious analyst should pretend that a single policy produces every change in national crime. Crime rates are influenced by many factors, including local policing strategies, prosecution decisions, economic conditions, demographics, and community involvement. Preliminary survey results also cannot establish a definitive cause-and-effect relationship.

But policy choices matter. A president who makes securing the border a priority, removes violent illegal aliens who are subject to deportation, directs the Justice Department to cooperate with the nation’s approximately 18,000 police departments, 3,400 sheriffs’ offices, and 2,300 elected district attorneys, funds law enforcement, and supports victims is sending a clear message: the government’s first responsibility is to protect the innocent.

>>> Another Win for the Task Force To Eliminate Fraud

That message matters. Criminals should expect enforcement, not indulgence. Police officers should know that federal officials recognize the risks they face. Prosecutors should have the resources and cooperation necessary to hold dangerous offenders accountable. Victims should not be treated as an afterthought in a system more concerned with the comfort of defendants than the security of communities.

“This report is proof that President Trump’s ’Make America Safe Again’ agenda is working,” Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward said, the No. 3 official in the Justice Department.

The statement captures the broader significance of the data, even if conclusions should await final estimates: public safety improves when government treats it as a core mission rather than a campaign slogan.

The lesson is straightforward. Effective enforcement, cooperation among federal, state, and local authorities, secure borders, adequately funded police departments, and meaningful support for victims are not outdated ideas. They are practical necessities.

Americans should celebrate these preliminary gains while remaining vigilant. The goal is not merely to report that crime has fallen. The goal is to ensure that it stays down—and that every community, regardless of size or location, receives the protection its residents deserve.

#7598. The Surprising New Guardians Of Liberty And What It Means For The Left

For years, the Left assumed Gen Z would be its most loyal supporters. Young Americans were expected to embrace socialism, distrust our institutions, and see government as the answer to the challenges facing our generation. But that assumption is increasingly being challenged by young people questioning the Left’s worldview and rediscovering the principles that made America exceptional.

The Left’s response has been revealing. Rather than defend its ideas, some of its most prominent voices are threatening the young Americans who dare to oppose them.

Recent remarks by Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-MI) offer a particularly alarming example.

Speaking about holding Trump administration officials accountable, Slotkin described using corruption cases to deter young Americans from joining the administration. She said she wanted prospective employees to worry that serving the Trump administration could mean buying themselves “a ton of problems.” Her stated goal was to discourage young people from getting involved.

Consider what that means for young Americans who want to serve their country by working for an administration, organization, or cause they believe in. The message is that choosing to build a career in the conservative movement could put a target on your back when the opposing side regains power.

>>> Dear Gen Z: Reagan Is Not a Relic

What an abhorrent message. Young Americans should be free to stand up for their convictions and pursue public service without fearing that their political affiliations could make them targets of the Left’s lawfare.

There is a world of difference between prosecuting actual criminal conduct and using the threat of prosecution to discourage participation in the political process. The justice system exists to enforce the law, not to intimidate political opponents or make an example of people whose political affiliations dissent from those in power.

Slotkin may frame her proposal as accountability. But when the stated objective is to deter young Americans from serving their nation, the question is whether the pursuit of justice is being conflated with the pursuit of political power.

Young Americans should find that deeply troubling, regardless of their political affiliation. And for a generation already questioning the Left’s vision for America, these remarks should prompt an even more fundamental question: Why should young people trust a political movement that seems willing to threaten their futures when they reject its ideas?

For years, the Left has presented socialism as a compassionate alternative to America’s founding principles. It promises equality through government control, security through dependence on the state, and progress through the expansion of political power. But beneath those promises lies a fundamental disagreement about human nature, individual liberty, and the proper role of government.

The American experiment rests on a different premise: that our rights come from our Creator, not the government, and that individuals—not political elites—should have the freedom to direct their own lives. Free enterprise, limited government, individual responsibility, and strong families are not outdated obstacles to progress. They are essential to preserving a free and prosperous society.

Socialism asks Americans to place greater trust in government. The American tradition asks government to respect the freedom and dignity of its citizens. One concentrates power in political institutions; the other recognizes that power must be limited to protect individual liberty.

For Gen Z, this is more than an abstract ideological debate. It is a question of what kind of country we want them to inherit—and whether they will be free to shape its future. Will they embrace a system that increasingly looks to government to direct society, or defend a nation built on the belief that individuals should be free to pursue their own aspirations?

The growing willingness of young Americans to challenge the Left’s assumptions should be welcomed as a sign of a healthy republic. No generation is obligated to accept socialism simply because it is presented as compassionate or inevitable. Young Americans have every right to question the Left’s promises, reject its prescriptions, and choose a different path.

>>> The Cost of Growing Up: Why Gen Z Feels Priced Out of the American Dream

At The Heritage Foundation, I see why preparing the next generation to defend America’s founding principles matters. Those principles do not survive on their own. They depend on young Americans who understand what is at stake and are willing to stand up for individual liberty, free enterprise, and limited government—even when doing so puts them at odds with the prevailing political culture.

Conservatives must make that case with conviction. We must demonstrate why the American tradition offers a better vision than the Left’s growing faith in government power. We must also ensure young Americans have the confidence and knowledge to defend that vision on their campuses and in their communities.

But the Left must answer for its own conduct. If its ideas are so compelling, why respond to young Americans who reject them with threats of prosecution? If socialism offers a better future, why should its advocates fear a generation willing to challenge it?

Slotkin’s remarks expose the danger of a political movement that increasingly treats ideological opposition as something to suppress rather than an argument to win. The threat is not simply that young Americans may be discouraged from joining an administration. It is that political participation itself could become a source of fear when the wrong people hold power.

Gen Z does not owe the Left its allegiance, and no political movement has the right to intimidate young Americans into submission.

The future of the American experiment depends on a generation willing to think independently, reject failed ideologies, and defend the freedoms that make this country exceptional. If the Left cannot win that generation through its ideas, it has no business trying to scare it into silence.

#7597. Religious Liberty, Terrorist Ideology, and the Limits of School Choice

Last year, Texas enacted one of the country's most expansive school-choice policies. The Texas Education Freedom Accounts program now serves more than 100,000 students, enabling families to choose the learning environments that align with their values and best meet their children’s learning needs.

School choice at this scale is worth celebrating. School-choice policies reflect the Constitution’s commitment to religious liberty and America’s longstanding recognition that parents, not the state, are the primary educators of their children.

A century ago, the Supreme Court struck down a Ku Klux Klan-backed Oregon law that would have banned private schooling, ruling in Pierce v. Society of Sisters that “the child is not the mere creature of the state.” Parents, the Court recognized, have the right and primary authority “to direct the upbringing and education” of their children.

Half a century later, in Yoder v. Wisconsin, the Court reaffirmed the “fundamental interest of parents to guide the religious future and education of their children.” The Court declared that only “interests of the highest order” can override these fundamental freedoms.

The Espinoza v. Montana Department of Revenue (2020) and Carson v. Makin (2022) decisions built on that foundation, holding that states cannot exclude otherwise qualified private schools from generally available scholarship programs merely because they are religious. The Court ruled that such discrimination is “odious to the Constitution.”

But Texas policymakers are now facing a question that school-choice advocates cannot avoid: What if parents choose schools funded by foreign adversaries that indoctrinate students to hate people who are not like them, and whose founders and staff have documented ties to terrorist organizations?

>>> School Choice Is About Religious Liberty, Not Just Better Test Scores

What is the limit of school choice?

Earlier this year, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott drew a line when he declared: “There’s no school choice for schools with ties to organizations that have connections to terrorism.” Several months earlier, Abbott had designated the Muslim Brotherhood and the Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR) as foreign terrorist organizations. (CAIR is challenging that designation.)

After those designations, acting comptroller Kelly Hancock wrote to Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton asking whether schools with ties to those organizations or the Chinese government could be excluded from the TEFA program. Paxton’s reply was unambiguous: “Let me be crystal clear: Texans’ tax dollars should never fund Islamic terrorists or America’s enemies.” Hancock then announced no schools with such ties would receive Texas tax dollars through TEFA.

That principle—that public funds should not flow to schools with ties to terrorist organizations or hostile foreign powers—is sound. All freedoms have limits. Liberty is not license. A state has a compelling interest in ensuring that taxpayer dollars do not subsidize the indoctrination of children to hate America or to support terrorism.

But even the soundest principle can be implemented in an unsound, or even unconstitutional manner.

In March 2026, Houston-area attorney and father Mehdi Cherkaoui filed a federal lawsuit against Paxton, Hancock, and Texas Education Commissioner Mike Morath, alleging that state officials had “systematically targeted Islamic schools for exclusion based on their religious identity.” His complaint observed that as of early 2026, hundreds of private schools across Texas—including numerous Christian schools—had been approved for TEFA, while not a single accredited Islamic school had been admitted. Cherkaoui sought to use TEFA funds to cover his children’s tuition at the Houston Quran Academy, but the school was not approved under the program. Three Islamic schools and additional parents joined a second suit shortly thereafter.

State officials denied the discrimination charge, explaining to the court that the comptroller’s office “had issues with processing and reviewing schools accredited by the nonprofit Cognia, regardless of whether they have Islamic affiliations.”

U.S. District Judge Alfred H. Bennett was not satisfied with that explanation. On March 17, hours before the original application deadline, he issued a temporary restraining order. At the emergency hearing, Bennett called the complete absence of approved Islamic schools “troubling,” remarking: “If you were to roll dice in a game of chance… you would not come up with those numbers. The appearance of this reeks.” He extended the student application deadline to March 31 and ordered state officials to receive and process applications from Islamic schools through the normal TEFA process. Within days, four Islamic schools were admitted: Brighter Horizons Academy in Garland, Bayaan Academy, Excellence Academy near Plano, and the Houston Quran Academy.

If it is true that the Muslim schools were not approved solely due to their religious affiliation, that would be a clear violation of their First Amendment rights. The Constitution’s guarantee of religious liberty undoubtedly prohibits such blanket discrimination.

However, the story is not so clear-cut. Two of the four schools now receiving TEFA funds—Brighter Horizons and the Houston Quran Academy—are at the center of serious, documented concerns regarding their institutional histories and affiliations.

Brighter Horizons Academy, based in Garland, is a subsidiary of the Islamic Services Foundation. According to a detailed investigation by the Middle East Forum (MEF), the school was established in part by Rasmi Almallah, who served on the board of the Holy Land Foundation—the largest terrorism financing operation in American history—and was named an unindicted co-conspirator in its 2008 federal trial.

ISF’s 2001 tax filings listed Mufid Abdelqader, a convicted HLF official and the brother of senior Hamas leader Khaled Mishal, as vice-president. His niece, Sarah Abdulqader, is currently a teacher at Brighter Horizons, and MEF notes that she “has been a passionate supporter of her convicted Hamas-financing father.” Previous staff reportedly included ISF director Nabil Sadoun, the lead author of ISF textbooks used at Brighter Horizons, a Jordanian Islamist activist whom the Dallas Morning News reported was “deported from the United States in 2010 for concealing Hamas ties on immigration paperwork.”

Some content in those ISF textbooks, used at Brighter Horizons and numerous other Islamic schools, is deeply troubling. According to MEF, one textbook teaches children ages seven and eight that non-Muslims are “the worst of creatures.” Another stresses the importance of jihad [the war against non-believers], stating: “When Muslims gave up jihad, did not abide by God’s will, started fighting among themselves and were submissive in the face of their enemies, God caused them to suffer greatly by allowing them to be dominated by those who do not fear Him or have any mercy for Islam.” The textbooks praise figures listed as unindicted co-conspirators in the Holy Land Foundation terror financing trial, including one who “describes suicide bombers and Hamas terrorists as ‘freedom fighters’ and ‘martyrs.’”

The school’s foreign funding adds another dimension. The Foundation for Defense of Democracies reported that Brighter Horizons received approximately $995,000 from the Islamic Development Bank for construction and expansion. Iran, a U.S.-designated state sponsor of terrorism, holds a significant capital share in the Islamic Development Bank and has representation on its governing board. During the Second Intifada, the bank directly managed funds that were paid to families of Palestinian terrorists who had been killed, injured, or imprisoned.

The Houston Quran Academy is operated by the Muslim American Society’s Katy Center (MAS). Federal prosecutors have described MAS as “the overt arm of the Muslim Brotherhood in the United States.” The academy’s principal, Hamed Ghazali, also chairs MAS’s Council of Islamic Schools. In 1988, Ghazali appeared to solicit funds for organizations later found to have financed Hamas. The next year, he “openly defended calls for the killing of Salman Rushdie.” In 2019, members of Congress called for an investigation into a MAS Philadelphia branch after it hosted an event in which children sang about torturing and beheading Jews.

>>> Stop Writing Blank Checks to Campuses That Protect Hate

These are not isolated cases. Middle East Forum data counts almost 800 Islamic educational initiatives across the United States, of which a clear majority are under Islamist control. Ninety of these institutions are in Texas, and several dozen may benefit from the new school subsidy program. Across those schools, MEF investigators found staff members who have shared Hamas propaganda, praised convicted terrorists, called for the destruction of America, and had children pledge loyalty to the Iranian supreme leader. Much of this infrastructure is tied to foreign money and foreign movements.

These are investigative findings, not criminal convictions against the schools themselves. But they are serious enough that state officials were right to ask questions. The comptroller’s supposed initial approach—a blanket exclusion of all Islamic schools—collides with the Constitution’s guarantee of free exercise of religion. Judge Bennett was right to find that troubling. But a blanket approval driven by litigation is also troubling.

The solution to an overbroad exclusion is not a rubber stamp, but due diligence. States must comply with the Constitution while protecting against terrorism. That requires examining each applicant school on its own record. Some Islamic schools clearly should qualify for the TEFA program. Whether Brighter Horizons and the Houston Quran Academy belong there is a harder question, and one the state should be able to answer through genuine investigation rather than blanket exclusion or court-compelled approval.

States should provide families access to robust school-choice options while protecting religious liberty. State officials should also take their duty seriously to avoid funding schools with genuine ties to terrorism. Those goals are not mutually exclusive. They require only that officials be precise, consistent, and willing to do their homework.

#7596. Freedom Isn’t Automatic—Each Generation Must Fight To Keep It

President Ronald Reagan’s famous warning that “Freedom is never more than one generation away from extinction; it has to be fought for and defended by each generation” is even more relevant today than when he first said it.

He correctly identified that prosperity is not a predetermined outcome. It is created and sustained by culture, institutions, and economic freedom, and it must therefore be the responsibility of every generation to protect and preserve it.

The comforting but misguided belief in economic determinism—holding that prosperity is determined by geography, natural resources, or historical circumstances—must be rejected. By this logic, the United States was destined to be a superpower simply because it occupies a resource-rich continent and is protected by two oceans.

Natural resources and geography may create opportunities, but they do not guarantee prosperity. History shows that Americans have intentionally pursued free enterprise, transparent institutions, and a limited federal government system that transformed opportunity into prosperity and allowed the nation to flourish.

The myth of economic determinism can be revealed by one of history’s most compelling natural experiments: North Korea and South Korea. The stark development trajectories between the two is evidence that political choices impact national outcomes. After World War II, North and South shared a common culture, language, geography, and history, yet chose dramatically different political and economic systems.

>>> The Surprising New Guardians Of Liberty And What It Means For The Left

South Korea embraced free enterprise, international trade, and economic liberation. North Korea adopted central planning, state ownership, and authoritarian rule. One developed into one of the world’s most advanced economies with residents enjoying personal freedoms and prosperity, while the other remains impoverished and isolated.

This contrast is even visible from space. Satellite photographs show South Korea illuminated at night by extensive infrastructure and a vibrant city, while North Korea remains dark due to an undeveloped power grid, poor infrastructure, and political factors that prioritize military needs over civilian energy consumption.

Geography didn’t create that divergence—communist policies did.

Similarly, Venezuela was among the wealthiest nations in Latin America for much of the 20th century, driven by large oil reserves. If natural resources guaranteed prosperity, it would be among the richest countries today. Instead, Venezuela fell from one of the most prosperous South American countries to one of the least prosperous in the world, with the Fraser Institute’s Economic Freedom Index ranking Venezuela number 22nd globally in 1980 and number 165th in 2021.

In less than half a century, empty promises made by socialist policymakers and enacted big-government policies undermined Venezuela’s economic foundation. The Manhattan Institute finds three policies implemented by dictator Hugo Chavez responsible for the nation’s widespread economic and humanitarian crisis: “nationalization of private industry, currency and price controls, and the fiscally irresponsible expansion of welfare programs.”

Chavez first nationalized agriculture by taking wealth and property from landowners and giving it to workers—leading to mismanagement and destruction of those resources. He then implemented controls to keep prices artificially low, which pushed out remaining firms and led to nationalized central authority. Finally, he expanded welfare programs purported to address poverty, educational shortcomings, and healthcare; all financed through high taxation and currency printing to the point of hyperinflation.

Inflation spiked, shortages of food and medicine became commonplace, government dependence increased, investment collapsed, and millions emigrated out of the country in search of better opportunities.

>>> The Conservative Coalition We Need to Save the West

But remember, in 1998 Chavez was democratically elected president. He campaigned on providing relief to poor- and middle-class populations by redistributing oil wealth in the form of social services—awfully similar to the “tax the rich” slogans of American socialists today. What starts with government programs, free buses, and artificially lower grocery prices ends with centralized authority, overreach, and the very socialist regimes that have killed citizens and destroyed entire countries in practice.

The lesson is that prosperity depends on policy—and this fact is increasingly relevant in the United States.

Socialist ideology has already made its way to America’s blue cities, with the youth driving this ideological shift from capitalism to socialism. Their affordability grievances are real, yet history repeatedly demonstrates that concentrated power in the hands of the state risks liberty, innovation, and long-term prosperity.

America’s future is not guaranteed. It depends on whether future generations defend and renew the principles and economic systems that historically made America great. Individual freedoms, economic mobility, and national prosperity should not be considered expectations, but rather privileges of ordered policies and culture.

That’s why policymakers and citizens must constantly, intentionally agitate for limited and constitutional government, a strong rule of law, and free enterprise to secure America’s future—because as Reagan reminded us, economic destiny is not guaranteed. It’s fought for and won time and time again.

#7594. How To Win Back the Disillusioned American Dream

Conservatives often assume socialism is easy to defeat. After all, the failing historical record of central planning and the economic success of free markets are on their side. But that hasn’t stopped socialism from gaining ground, particularly among young Americans.

A Fox News poll finds that while 72% of Democrats under the age of 45 believe capitalism is not working well, 66% think moving to socialism would be a good idea. Those numbers should concern any American who values economic freedom.

Many older conservatives immediately respond by pointing to the Soviet Union, Venezuela, or Cuba as evidence of the horrors of socialism. They’re not wrong, but they’re not addressing the question young voters are actually asking.

Young people are choosing socialism not because they hate America, but because they believe the once reliable American Dream is out of reach. Homeownership is becoming unattainable. Student debt delays major life decisions. Family formation is becoming more expensive every year. Upward mobility seems impossible when wages barely outpace inflation.

Their frustration is real, and though the promises of socialism are empty, those of capitalism—or at least what they think is capitalism—have gone unfulfilled.

The median sales price of a new home was over $410,000 in 2025, nearly five times the median household income, a ratio almost twice as high as in 1980. Student loans cost the average new graduate hundreds of dollars per month. And despite inflation coming down from pandemic peaks, 3.4% CPI eats away at weekly paychecks.

>>> The Cost of Growing Up: Why Gen Z Feels Priced Out of the American Dream

Simply put, the cost of adulthood has become unaffordable for millions of young Americans.

Socialists have recognized this reality, and though their proposed solutions are economically unsustainable, at least they acknowledge the problem. And too often, conservatives are quick to condemn socialism without addressing the underlying reasons why Gen Z finds it attractive.

Socialists blame capitalism for modern economic hardship, but the affordability crisis should not be treated as evidence that competitive capitalism is failing America’s youth. In most sectors burdening young Americans, competition has been weakened by government intervention, political favoritism, and policies that distort prices and restrict supply.

Look at housing. For decades, local governments restricted development with zoning regulations, permitting delays, and other barriers to construction. Simultaneously, government-backed mortgage policies increased purchasing power without addressing supply shortages. Then, politicians responded to rising costs with rent control and rent freezes that further distorted the market and drove up homeownership costs.

It’s no surprise, then, that the average age of a first-time homebuyer is at an all-time high of 40.

Next, look to higher education. Government-backed student lending has enabled colleges to raise prices. The result is a system that saddles students with tens to hundreds of thousands of dollars of debt and politicians that propose student loan forgiveness or other subsidies as the solution—which neither adds value to the credential, lowers the cost of providing education, nor changes the broken mechanism behind why college tuition is so expensive.

The housing and college markets are not examples of a free market operating properly. They reflect government-created scarcity, regulatory dysfunction, and cronyism.

Therefore, cost-of-living concerns facing Gen Z should not be used as evidence that competitive capitalism is a failed model—especially when most economic problems stem from policies fundamentally opposed to the free market.

For policymakers, this means acknowledging Gen Z’s reasonable concerns and showing them how freedom, not government control, can improve life.

>>> The Surprising New Guardians Of Liberty And What It Means For The Left

When conservatives respond to rising socialist affiliation only by warning about unsuccessful experiments, they fail to address the affordability problems people experience every day, which are driving this ideological shift.

The average American is not watching lectures on the historical failures of central planning or reading through textbooks comparing the economic philosophies of Karl Marx and Adam Smith. Young Americans are instead trying to make monthly rent payments, budget to buy a house, pay back student loans, and afford groceries—all while entering adulthood, starting a career, and raising a family.

So, a successful conservative strategy must both demonstrate how free-market policies solve modern problems and expose the socioeconomic failures of socialism.

This means increasing housing supply, removing government distortions in housing and other markets, lowering barriers to entrepreneurship, promoting energy abundance, reducing regulatory burdens, and making family formation more affordable. Most importantly, Americans need evidence that economic freedom reliably produces upward mobility.

The greatest victories against socialism were never won through slogans, but through prosperity. When people can afford homes, start businesses, raise families, and build wealth, socialism loses its appeal. But when those opportunities disappear, socialism gains favor.

The future debate over socialism won’t be won by arguing endlessly about 20th-century failed experiments in foreign nations. It will be won by proving that economic freedom can still deliver opportunity and prosperity for all Americans in the 21st century.

#7593. New York’s Property Tax Hike Chases Wealthy Wallets Away

New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani faces an uphill battle balancing the city’s budget while ushering in his very expensive socialist utopia. But rest assured: New public bathrooms and free opera tickets are still coming, and the ultra-wealthy will foot the bill. Or so the plan goes. Predictably, his “tax the rich” mantra is already going beyond New York socialites.

With the pied-à-terre tax implemented in July, property owners and investors who simply maintain a secondary residence in one of the city’s boroughs are subject to a new property tax surcharge. New York Gov. Kathy Hochul proposed it on April 15 to help close the city’s budget gap—the same day Mr. Mamdani posted a video outside Citadel CEO Ken Griffin’s $238 million penthouse, naming him as an example.

The legislature approved the measure on May 27, and it took effect on July 1. It expires June 30, 2031, unless renewed. In the first phase, which runs through mid-2028, condos and co-ops valued at $1 million or more face new, steep tax rates of 4% to 6.5%. For context, New York state’s average effective property tax rate in 2024 was 1.3% and Manhattan’s was 0.71%.

Mr. Mamdani’s “fair share” philosophy includes a quintupling of property taxes on thousands of people. After that initial phase, the surcharge threshold rises to $5 million with lower rates of 0.8% to 1.3% applying to all non-primary residences, exempting housing units under arm’s length leases of at least one year.

>>> No, Mamdani, Socialism Does Not Increase Affordability

Even these lower rates will double people’s property taxes. Furthermore, the lower rates are designed to be offset by new valuation methods being cooked up by the city Department of Finance to increase the assessed value of properties.

The rollout was messy from the start, when the city published a list of 900,000 high-value properties along with many of the owners’ full names. The city appeared to adopt a kind of guilty-until-proven-innocent tax liability, making residents argue they aren’t subject to the pied- à-terre tax. Owners were left with confusion and a loss of privacy.

Since Manhattan has roughly 16,700 condos and co-ops valued above the $1 million threshold, it will be hit hardest by this tax. Secondary residents will owe an average surcharge of $68,559 each year. Brooklyn also shows significant exposure, with the outer boroughs coming in at smaller counts.

New York projects the measure will raise about $500 million in annual revenue. But that assumes the owners stay. Revenue could easily fall by tens of millions of dollars if some owners leave and sell off their secondary residences, which is why wealth taxes elsewhere have repeatedly fallen short of projections. Each property owner who leaves the city shrinks the tax base.

Ultimately, this is a tax on investment in New York real estate with ramifications that will affect even middle-class New Yorkers. Picture a wealthy Californian considering a second residence on the East Coast. At Phase One’s top condo rates, a unit in Manhattan with a $5 million assessed value—the median Manhattan residence is more than $1 million—now has an extra $262,500 tax bill, simply because his primary residence is elsewhere.

>>> Mamdani’s City Grocery Plan Could Leave Taxpayers Paying for Every Banana

Suddenly, Cape Cod and Miami look a lot more attractive, so the wealthy begin taking their spending elsewhere. Local businesses lose sales and need fewer employees. The Real Estate Board of New York argued before the State Legislature that the surcharge would discourage development, reduce construction jobs and drive high-end buyers to other cities.

Supporters argue the tax discourages luxury units from sitting vacant, hence the one-year-lease exemption. But that’s not where New York’s housing crisis is. Very few people can afford $5,000 a month for a one-bedroom apartment downtown. Filling a few luxury units won’t change that.

Legal fights are well underway, and while a Staten Island judge called the rollout “arbitrary and capricious,” the process was ordered to be redone, not canceled entirely. None of the legal challenges has succeeded in striking down the tax itself.

Part-time residents already pay taxes to fund city services, and these surcharges will incentivize those folks to leave, reducing revenue from the surcharge as well as existing taxes. As the more mobile wealthy flee for greener pastures in low-tax states, the burden of funding Mr. Mamdani’s socialist utopia will increasingly have to fall on the less mobile middle class.

#7592. Wise Words from Third Circuit Judge Stephanos Bibas as to Access to Court Records

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

My Stanford law school colleagues Nora and David Engstrom, as well as Berkeley law professor Jonah Gelbach and others, have asked the Advisory Committee on Civil Rules recommend a new Rule of Civil Procedure (5.3) governing the sealing of court records. I think this is an excellent idea: While there is a good deal of precedent on the question, distilling it into a rule that can easily be consulted by judges, lawyers, law clerks, and pro se litigants would be very helpful.

Just today, Third Circuit Judge Stephanos Bibas (also a former law professor), submitted a letter endorsing the proposed rule, and I thought it was much worth passing along:

Dear Members of the Advisory Committee on Civil Rules:

I write to express my strong support for proposed Rule 5.3, a much-needed recapitulation of the procedural standards governing sealing of judicial records.

The public has a presumptive right to access judicial records. This right serves several important societal functions. By exposing the records of private wrongdoing to the public eye, this right deters further wrongdoing. By forcing the government to litigate out in the open, it empowers the public "to keep a watchful eye on the workings of public agencies." Nixon v. Warner Commc'ns, Inc., 435 U.S. 589, 598 (1978). And by enabling the public to dig into the bases for judicial decisions, it enables the public to assure itself of the strength of judicial reasoning, the cornerstone of judicial legitimacy. This right thus not only "diminishes possibilities for injustice, incompetence, perjury, and fraud," but also provides "the public with a more complete understanding of the judicial system and a better perception of its fairness." In re Avandia Mktg., Sales Prac. & Prod. Liab. Litig., 924 F.3d 662, 672 (3d Cir. 2019) (internal quotation marks omitted).

On paper, this right looks strong. In the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit, where I sit, a district court issuing an order to seal "must articulate the compelling, countervailing interests to be protected" and "make specific findings on the record concerning the effects of disclosure." Id. (internal quotation marks omitted). But that standard is a paper tiger—mighty in appearance, but toothless in practice. Time and again, we see cases on appeal where the parties asked to seal large parts of the record below, and the district court, with little discussion, agreed to do so.

Take one recent motion to seal in a Third Circuit case. The district court had certified a multi-state class action against a car company. On appeal, the company asked us to seal ten volumes of appendices, totaling nearly three thousand pages of material. The company told us that sealing was necessary to prevent competitors from copying its design choices, stealing its engineering solutions, and exploiting its sales strategy.

But it took only a cursory glance at the appendices to see how overbroad the company's request was. Hundreds of pages, for example, covered deposition testimony from one of the plaintiff's lay witnesses, a mechanic who had worked on the defendant's cars and had commented on their alleged defects. Hundreds of other pages dealt with one of the plaintiffs' experts, who had opined on the veracity of the defendant's public comments and sales catalogues. But if the mechanic based his testimony on his day-to-day work on the defendant's cars, and the expert had based his testimony on the company's public statements, how would these materials reveal competitive secrets? So I denied the request without prejudice, asking the company to come back with a narrower request if it so chose. But why had the record below been sealed in the first place?

It should come as little surprise that motions to seal almost always go unopposed. The harm of overbroad sealing falls on future victims of repeat tortfeasors, future litigants in related cases, and the public at large. It does not fall on the parties to the case.

Indeed, the parties generally have an active interest in secrecy. The party who moves to seal records fears that the information produced in the case could lead to bad press coverage, competitive harms, or even follow-on litigation. The other party presumably does not share those same concerns about broad disclosure, but it does not share the public's concerns about overbroad sealing, either.

So in the give-and-take game of litigation, where it can be important to reserve your capital for fighting the fights that matter to your client, opposing a motion to seal is a waste of that capital. At the very least, it is a waste of time and money. For lawyers in an active dispute—so used to viewing themselves as only agents of their clients, and not also officers of the court—submitting an opposition to an overbroad motion to seal might not seem worth the cost of the paper to print it.

This leaves it to district-court judges to police these motions and protect the public's presumptive right of access to judicial records. But what my experience as a judge on the court of appeals has taught me, Professor Engstrom et. al's empirical work now confirms: Most district courts rubber-stamp these requests.

This might come as a surprise to some members of the Judicial Conference. After all, the law of every circuit requires district courts to reject requests to seal that are too broad to be justified by their supposed rationale.

So why do district courts frequently fail to apply that law? One problem might be the lack of developed precedent in this area. Because motions to seal are almost never subject to full treatment in district court opinions, let alone appellate review, there are few decisions applying legal standards to specific facts, teasing out what interests suffice to justify sealing, and how broad is too broad. Without clearly factually analogous precedent to rely on, district courts might be more hesitant to deny a motion to seal as overbroad, even though the operative legal standard compels that result.

Another problem is rooted in the lack of adversarial presentation. With no one on the other side, inflated claims of confidentiality go unchallenged.

Other problems might boil down to the mechanics of busy district court dockets. Perhaps, for example, when a district court grants a protective order, that decision generates an inertial force that skews the outcome of the subsequent motion to seal, even though the two decisions are subject to different legal standards. Or perhaps a motion to seal, because it is unopposed, slips under the radar, resembling an administrative matter to be rubber-stamped rather than a legal decision to be carefully scrutinized.

But whatever the reason, the results are clear: For most motions to seal, "the parties agree, the busy district court accommodates, and nobody is left in the courtroom to question whether the decision satisfied the substantive requirements." Binh Hoa Le v. Exeter Fin. Corp., 990 F.3d 410, 417 (5th Cir. 2021).

This proposed rule will push parties and courts alike to do better. First, this proposed rule will ensure that the parties know what their obligations are when they submit a motion to seal. I often sit by designation on the District of Delaware, where I regularly receive motions to seal with no accompanying explanation or justification, putting the onus on me to push the parties for more. Under Proposed Rule 5.3(c), parties will be reminded that, as our circuit has regularly held, "[b]road allegations of harm, bereft of specific examples or articulated reasoning, are insufficient." In re Avandia Mktg., 924 F.3d at 673 (internal quotation marks omitted).

Second, this proposed rule will act as a process-forcing mechanism for busy district court judges. District courts lack the benefit of adversarial litigation over motions to seal. And without a party opposing a motion, it is easy to think that no reasoning is needed for an order—if no party loses, the thinking goes, no party needs a basis for the court's decision.

Proposed Rule 5.3(h) makes clear that even without an adversarial party, the district court must act as the steward of the public interest in accessing court records, and must reason through its decision. The decision to seal is for the court to make by applying the correct legal standard, not for the parties to make by means of consent. Proposed Rule 5.3(i) provides a checklist that a district court can use in reaching that decision.

Finally, the proposed rule will remind parties and district courts alike that sealing is not an all-or-nothing question. Proposed Rule 5.3(d)(3) and (g) make clear that, where viable, the default approach should be targeted redactions. The choice is not between disclosing a list of social security numbers and sealing an entire document. A happy medium is often readily available.

This proposed rule does not make new law. Sunlight is the best disinfectant for many societal ills, yet sealing "insulates the participants" in the legal process, "masking impropriety, obscuring incompetence, and concealing corruption." Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corp. v. F.T.C., 710 F.2d 1165, 1179 (6th Cir. 1983). Judicial reasoning is the basis for judicial legitimacy, yet sealing "withdraws an element of the judicial process from public view," making "the ensuing decision look more like fiat." Matter of Krynicki, 983 F.2d 74, 75 (7th Cir. 1992) (Easterbrook, J.). For these reasons, the courts of appeals have consistently held that the public has a presumptive right to access judicial records, one that should only be abrogated where necessary, and even there only to the extent necessary. This proposed rule simply makes that right harder to neglect.

My then-student Jennifer Welson and I had unsuccessfully proposed a sealing rule to the Rule Committee in 2020, on behalf of the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press and Electronic Frontier Foundation; but I much hope that the Engstrom et al. proposal, which is backed by considerably more empirical research than mine had been, will be more successful.

#7589. Fifth Circuit on Pseudonymity of Libel Defendant (Who Claims She Was Sexually Assaulted)

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From Doe v. Roe, decided today by Fifth Circuit Judges Jennifer Walker Elrod, Carolyn Dineen King, and Carl Stewart:

After receiving notice of Jane Roe's impending California lawsuit involving allegations of sexual assault and sexual harassment, John Doe sued Roe in the Southern District of Mississippi, alleging that Roe was attempting to extort and defame him. Roe moved to proceed pseudonymously in the Mississippi lawsuit. The district court denied her permission to do so. Roe appeals that decision, raising several concerns with the district court's analysis. Because we agree with some of Roe's arguments, we vacate and remand for the district court to reconsider whether Roe should be allowed to proceed pseudonymously….

Roe argues that allegations of sexual assault involve matters of the utmost intimacy [and can thus justify pseudonymity]. We agree. There is no doubt that requiring alleged rape and sexual assault victims to proceed "under their real identities would require them to disclose information of the utmost intimacy." It is no surprise, then, that numerous courts have allowed alleged victims of sexual misconduct to proceed under a pseudonym, "including when they are defendants being sued for libel and related torts."

We agree with Roe. To start, we are not persuaded that the proverbial cat is out of the bag here. True, publicly available information cannot be obscured by courts. However, that internet sleuths might speculate that Roe is a particular person because her California complaint "lines up with [her] public profile" is not the same as a public broadcasting of Roe's certain identity. As to the fact that Roe's name was a matter of public record for short periods, that was either because of Doe's actions (which Roe objected to), or Roe's inadvertent disclosures which counsel corrected and constituted no waiver (which we address below)….

Last, Roe argues that she did not waive her right to proceed anonymously. Again, we agree. Roe never waived her ability to request pseudonymity because her conduct does not constitute an "intentional relinquishment" of that position. Roe's opposition to Doe's motion to proceed pseudonymously waived nothing because Roe's position was that she should be allowed to proceed pseudonymously while he should not be. And any confusion about Roe's position based on the precise language in her opposition brief was clarified by her own subsequent motions seeking to seal or redact Doe's amended complaint (which used Roe's real name) and to proceed pseudonymously.

Further, Doe's use of Roe's real name in open court did not constitute waiver on Roe's behalf because, at the time, Doe had already publicly named Roe in his amended complaint, Roe had a pending motion seeking to seal or redact that amended complaint naming her, and Roe objected to the use of her name at the hearing (even if not as fast as a prudent attorney likely should have). Finally, we are not convinced that Roe's inadvertent disclosures of her real name in the California case and on this appeal constitute waiver. The disclosures were unintentional, were made in portions of larger filings, and Roe took steps to correct the errors once becoming aware of them, resulting in the sealing and refiling of the documents. These facts do not demonstrate that Roe intentionally relinquished her request to proceed pseudonymously….

In light of the clarifications provided in this opinion, we find that it is appropriate to allow the district court to reconsider whether Roe should be permitted to proceed under a pseudonym in this case. {We acknowledge Doe's argument that allowing Roe to proceed under a pseudonym would be prejudicial to him. We think that argument is best left for the district court to address in the first instance on remand.}

The school’s leaders aim to present the vision for the law school to the Texas legislature in 2027, with the goal of opening in 2030.

In October 2025, the Paul L. Foster Family Foundation also announced a $5 million matching grant, and El Paso, Texas, law firm Tawney, Acosta & Chaparro committed to a $5 million gift in April. Other El Paso firms—including Farah Law, Flores Mendez Law, ScottHulse Attorneys at Law, and Dallas-based Kastl Law—have made donations that will be matched by the Woody and Gayle Hunt Family Foundation’s grant.

The law school would focus on public and private international law involving the United States and Mexico and aims to address the shortage of fluent bilingual lawyers.
