#7544. Two cheers for “insecure originalism”

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

In his new book, Justice Samuel Alito takes aim at what he calls judicial “insecurity,” or a judge’s self-conscious worry that he might be advancing his own policy preferences under the guise of impartial adjudication. “Twenty-first century originalists,” he argues, “should shed this insecure mindset.”

Alito’s suggestion is at odds with decades of conservative legal thought, including remarks by Justice Antonin Scalia. More fundamentally, what Alito labels insecurity is better understood as a form of humility and self-awareness. And that humility is laudable for all judges, not just originalists. There is much more to fear from the self-assured or overconfident judge than the insecure one.

In some of the book’s most discussed passages (and in an op-ed in The Wall Street Journal), Alito impugns “insecure originalism,” in part because “insecurity” may lead originalists “to worry that they are subconsciously engaging in ‘results-oriented’ decision-making and ‘judicial activism’ in the service of their own policy preferences.” Alito urges originalists to shrug off this worry: “Originalist judges should . . . be on guard against subconsciously setting a higher bar for legal arguments that yield outcomes they find desirable as a policy matter.”

The insecurity that Alito bemoans has a rich history that his discussion omits. In recent decades, the jurist most associated with this kind of thinking was longtime conservative hero Scalia. In his oft-repeated view, “The judge who always likes the results he reaches is a bad judge.” This maxim was admonitory. It not so subtly suggested that other judges, perhaps of the non-originalist variety, always liked where their theorizing led them. But not the principled originalist, whose impartial theory necessarily brought about disappointment – the price of integrity.

Scalia often fleshed out this line of thinking by pointing to specific issues that originalism resolved in ways he claimed to find regrettable. The First Amendment, in Scalia’s view, encompassed a right to burn the American flag, something that Scalia personally found distasteful. And the confrontation clause effectively demanded that many serious offenders go unpunished. Scalia’s critics sometimes chafed when he drew attention to these decisions, which seemed to give him permission to issue other rulings that did align with his own policy preferences.

Scalia’s disciples have long echoed his view of the “bad judge.” In published writings, including a judicial opinion, Justice Neil Gorsuch has favorably adapted Scalia’s “bad judge” admonition. And Justice Amy Coney Barrett made Scalia’s aphorism a prominent part of her recent memoir and related book tour. Barrett has also offered her own variations on this theme, remarking for instance: “You should sometimes be reaching results that you really dislike.” In a similar spirit, a majority opinion by Justice Brett Kavanaugh defended its own impartiality by adducing examples of standing decisions that cut in different ideological directions.

What Alito labels “insecurity” is really a judicial virtue and better characterized as a form of self-consciousness or rigor. When a judge realizes that he is consistently ruling for or against a particular kind of party, he has good reason to reflect on the possibility that he is the victim of his own biases. That point has special salience in today’s United States, which is marked by partisan polarization.

When a judge confronts a case with partisan valence, he would do well to pause over his own potential bias. In the context of contemporary federal judging, such a bias often correlates with the judge’s appointing president. A judge appointed by a Republican or Democratic president is likely to have personal views aligned with Republicans or Democrats, respectively. And the judge is likely to have a social set that is ideologically skewed. As Alito noted in an interview, such a skew may not be the judge’s doing, so much as the result of ideological backlash against the judge’s rulings. But even if unfair or unfortunate, the backlash’s effects are real.

In this context, a judge will be tempted to please his own ideological tribe while being insensitive to its rival. A Democratic-appointed judge may play to Bluesky, writing zingers in trendy language that please imagined audiences. Or a Republican-appointed judge may similarly look forward to standing ovations at Federalist Society galas. These incentives and trains of thought are not so hypothetical. And once this kind of behavior takes hold, the judges in question become more like partisan actors than principled defenders of either legal rules or the judiciary.

Against that backdrop, an anti-partisanship principle offers a means of reaching better, more accurate results – not a means of sacrificing accuracy for illicit ends. A judge who sensibly factors in his own partisan affiliation, background, or associations is more likely to identify and apply the law by his own lights. Or so one might hope. Whether anti-partisanship can work largely depends on how it is implemented.

There are many ways of implementing anti-partisanship, and different approaches may befit different scenarios or appeal to different jurists. Surely no judge should factor in party identity in a way that squarely contradicts the law’s dictates. And because many judges have sincere legal views with an ideological valence, complete anti-partisanship is both infeasible and undesirable. Yet judging often involves subtle choices. And those subtleties create room for the anti-partisanship principle to have meaningful effect.

At the Supreme Court, certiorari, that is, deciding what case to hear, affords perhaps the most immediate opportunity for discretionary judgments. Is a particular case or issue ripe for prompt consideration, or sufficiently worthy of the court’s attention? These questions yield judgment calls, and a judge may reasonably consider whether he is consistently making these decisions in favor of one party or ideology. Cert might be warranted only when a relatively objective test is satisfied, such as a deep circuit split. Or the justice might have a practice of avoiding expedited review in such cases.

Moreover, all appellate courts confront myriad opportunities to craft the scope and depth of their holdings. A judge who supports one broad holding after another in favor of his appointing president or party is probably ruling irresponsibly. That judge is not merely transgressing principles of minimalism (deciding only what needs to be decided) or gradualism (deciding incrementally) but doing so in an especially objectionable way by ruling grandly with partisan effect. By contrast, a humbler judge will be sure to wait beyond the first or second chance to resolve a major issue when that issue has a partisan valence.

Judges of all kinds also face an array of different grounds on which to rule. An anti-partisan judge might look with care at jurisdictional requirements or opportunities for abstention, adapting Alexander Bickel’s “passive virtues” (that is, pursuing an impassive strategy, rather than ruling either swiftly or grandly). Or he might shelve a holding in the alternative where a single, narrower holding would suffice.

Precedent affords additional opportunities for anti-partisanship. When a party seeks to overrule case law, a judge might ask whether that request has a partisan valence – and then look to see whether the request to overrule has broad, cross-ideological support.

Finally, judges may express themselves differently depending on the presence of partisan tensions. Barrett made this point in Trump v. Anderson, which (as to result) unanimously held that Colorado could not exclude then-candidate Trump from the presidential ballot based on section 3 of the 14th Amendment. She wrote separately to note that the court “has settled a politically charged issue in the volatile season of a Presidential election” and that, “[p]articularly in this circumstance, writings on the Court should turn the national temperature down, not up.” Thus, Anderson was “not the time to amplify disagreement with stridency.” In other contexts, judges may follow this general advice by muting their rhetoric or even suppressing dissents.

In our current polarized environment, it may be hard to imagine that a judge would be too anti-partisan. Yet Alito quite properly raises just that concern.

As Alito insightfully puts it: “insecure originalists may actually welcome occasions when their originalist analysis leads to results they dislike. When that occurs, they experience a gratifying frisson, a brief catharsis in which their anxiety about having unconsciously succumbed to the temptation of results-oriented decision-making is released.” The image here is of a judge who becomes so excited about proving his own impartiality that he becomes utterly partial.

Once again, Alito’s point is hardly limited to originalists, and other commentators have raised similar concerns about judging in general. For example, Judge Richard Posner once noted that “[i]t is a source of satisfaction to a judge to vote for the litigant who irritates him . . . for it is by doing such things that you know that you are playing the judge role.”

This kind of concern shows that the anti-partisanship principle must itself be deployed reflectively and cautiously. There is no one simple trick for impartial or accurate judging, and any maxim of juridical wisdom can be twisted or taken too much to heart.

Alito’s worry also indicates that the anti-partisanship principle has only contingent appeal. In a less polarized polity, partisanship might play a smaller or even a trivial role in judicial decision-making. In that environment, the anti-partisanship principle would not help – or might even worsen – judicial bias. But that is not our world today.

Alito elaborates his point in a way that further underscores the appeal of anti-partisanship. To wit, he notes that “an originalist judge should not cavalierly or happily embrace results that defy common sense.” Attention to common sense is indeed justifiable, but that is because (or if) it is truly “common.” Consensus views may well provide a helpful indication that a particular ruling is senseless, catastrophic, or absurd.

But “common sense” is not at all the same as Alito’s other and more salient subject – namely, “outcomes [judges] find desirable as a policy matter.” In placing these two ideas in successive paragraphs and casting them as comparable, Alito inadvertently reveals how easy it is for a judge to draw an equivalence between, or fail to differentiate, his own highly contestable views and genuine consensus.

Anti-partisanship may not be for everyone. The legal system may even benefit from having some judges in each court who align with one or the other of the nation’s two political parties. That arrangement would help partisans identify with the judiciary and might foster a kind of adversarial system within the third branch. But that picture seems appealing, if at all, only if the partisan judges remain the exception.

In a later chapter, Alito praises Judge Learned Hand’s famous speech on “the Spirit of Liberty.” Alito notes for instance: “I am convinced that the spirit of the Constitution—of limited but effective government, individual rights, and equal justice under law—is alive and well in the hearts of the American people.”

Alas, Alito’s discussion does not quote or acknowledge what Hand believed the spirit of liberty to be. In the speech’s most memorable and oft-repeated line, Hand posited: “The spirit of liberty is the spirit which is not too sure that it is right.”

One might say that the spirit of liberty is a bit insecure. The spirit of the Constitution is, too.

Richard M. Re is a professor at Harvard Law School. Early in his career, he clerked for then-Judge Brett M. Kavanaugh and Justice Anthony M. Kennedy.

#7542. Justices to decide whether failure to plead an affirmative defense prevents moving for summary judgment on that same defense

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

Younge v. Fulton Judicial Circuit District Attorney’s Office, Georgia, to be argued on Nov. 2, involves an issue that will quicken the pulse of civil procedure aficionados. No less than four different rules of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure are in play: affirmative defenses under Rule 8, amending a pleading under Rule 15, pretrial management under Rule 16, and summary judgment under Rule 56.

The case raising this cornucopia of pretrial procedural rules comes out of a relatively typical civil rights suit in which the plaintiff asserts that she was improperly dismissed from her job and is now suing for damages. Jasmine Younge held a high-level position in the Fulton County District Attorney’s Office for about two months until she was fired in July 2019 by District Attorney Paul Howard. Younge says she was dismissed from her job about two weeks after telling Howard that she was pregnant. Later that year, Younge sued the Fulton County District Attorney’s Office for a number of civil rights violations, including the claim that termination because of her pregnancy violated Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

The DA’s office answered the complaint, and pretrial proceedings ensued. Save for a few disputed matters, discovery closed in January 2022. About two months later, at a pretrial hearing on a discovery issue, the DA’s office informed the court and Younge that it intended to move for summary judgment, including on the basis of the personal-staff exemption defense, which it had not asserted in its answer. (Under Title VII, certain officials are exempted from the statutory definition of employee, including (1) members of an elected official’s “personal staff” and (2) “policymaking appointees.”) The DA’s office explained that it did not learn of the defense until its lawyer began drafting the summary judgment motion.

Soon after the March 2022 hearing, the DA’s office moved for summary judgment, citing its defenses based upon the statutory exemptions from Title VII in support of the motion. The DA never sought to amend its answer to add these defenses.

Younge objected to the motion, arguing as a procedural matter that it was too late for the DA’s office to assert new affirmative defenses. Her waiver argument regarding the personal-staff exemption was rejected several times in the lower courts, first by the federal magistrate judge who permitted the personal-staff defense to be asserted and recommended summary judgment in favor of the DA’s office predicated on that defense. The district court then agreed with this recommendation and entered judgment in favor of the DA. Next, the case was appealed to the United States Court of Appeals for the 11th Circuit.

The 11th Circuit (as had the lower courts) applied its reasoning in the 1988 case of Hassan v. U.S. Postal Service, in which it had employed a prejudice analysis to determine whether to allow the defendant to move for summary judgment based on an unpled affirmative defense. Here, the district court had determined that there was no prejudice to allowing the personal-staff defense. Significantly, in addition to finding that the DA’s office should prevail on the defense, the lower courts noted that Younge could not identify any additional discovery that she would have pursued had the defense been asserted earlier.

As the 11th Circuit summarized, “since Hassan, [i]t had repeatedly reaffirmed that a district court may receive evidence of an unpleaded affirmative defense if the plaintiff was not ‘prejudiced’ by the defendant’s failure to plead the defense in its answer.” Furthermore, the circuit court explained that “the record contains copious discovery evidence concerning each of the six factors” relevant to “the personal staff exemption.” Accordingly, the 11th Circuit affirmed the district court, finding that “Younge had not suffered prejudice from the DA’s Office’s late assertion of the personal staff exemption” and that summary judgment had properly been entered in favor of the DA.

The justices agreed to hear the case in March to determine whether an affirmative defense may be asserted as a basis for summary judgment if not presented earlier in a pleading.

In seeking reversal of the judgment below, Younge argues that the court should take a textualist approach to reading the applicable rules. “Rule 8(c)(1) emphasizes” without exception “that a defendant must plead ‘any’ affirmative defenses,” she states. Since the DA did not do so, it should not have been allowed to seek summary judgment on the basis of such an unpled defense.

Younge further argues that allowing a summary judgment motion based upon an unpled affirmative defense permits a defendant to circumvent the requirements of Rule 15(a)(2) for amending a pleading and Rule 16(b)(4) for modifying a scheduling order. The former requires a court to analyze a number of factors, including “undue delay” on the part of the party seeking to amend, and is stricter than a mere prejudice standard. The latter requires “good cause,” considers due diligence, and, again, is more demanding than just showing prejudice. Younge would then have the court set aside the 11th Circuit’s prejudice standard and apply the “well-established standards and procedures of Rules 15(a)(2) and 16(b)(4).”

The DA, on the other hand, stands by the prejudice standard set out in Hassan and applied by the 11th Circuit. It asserts that this standard is correct given the interrelated purposes of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure: to resolve cases on the merits and to avoid their resolution on the basis of technical or formalistic application of the rules themselves.

According to the DA, the text, structure, and historical development of the FRCP support this purposive reading of the rules. Regarding the text, the DA invokes Rule 61, the harmless error rule, which provides that “[a]t every stage of the proceeding, the court must disregard all errors and defects that do not affect any party’s substantial rights.” “Structurally,” the DA expresses that “the Rules impose limits on amending pleadings to import new factual issues … but not on raising legal arguments like the one the DA’s Office raised here.” And as for the history, the DA points out that “Rule 12 used to provide that a defendant waives all unpleaded defenses but no longer does.”

Overall, the purposive approach to interpreting the FRCP may prove especially appealing to the court: As the DA argues, the FRCP drew on and were influenced by the rules in the courts of equity, which aimed to simplify pleading rules and adopted a flexible approach to promote the resolution of cases on the merits. In pretrial matters such as pleadings and discovery, context – the underlying facts, the claims and defenses asserted, and the parties’ conduct, among other things – matters. Given this, although the court may not write broadly, I think it’s unlikely to find that the 11th Circuit’s prejudice standard was out of bounds.

Rodger D. Citron is the Associate Dean for Research and Scholarship and Professor of Law at Touro University, Jacob D. Fuchsberg Law Center.

#7540. New York State Bar Association tells lawyers not to bill for time saved by AI

The New York State Bar Association is calling for restrictions on how much lawyers can bill clients for the amount of time saved using artificial intelligence tools or expended learning how to use it. (Image from Shutterstock)

The New York State Bar Association is calling for restrictions on how much lawyers can bill clients for the amount of time saved using artificial intelligence tools or expended learning how to use it.

Law360 reported Monday that the state bar association’s Committee on Artificial Intelligence and Emerging Technologies issued a report classifying the cost of buying and maintaining such software as an overhead expense that can be passed along as a disbursement only when tied to a specific client matter and when the basis for the charge has been disclosed.

According to Law360, the report added that lawyers generally don’t have to tell clients about AI use for administrative tasks—such as word processing, spelling and grammar checks, calendaring or timekeeping—provided that the use doesn’t affect fees.

“Generative AI is indelibly changing the practice of law. As part of our mission to be the leading voice for the legal profession, we are providing clear guidelines on the use of AI tools as a resource, so attorneys can use AI responsibly and ethically in their practices,” said Taa Grays, the president of the New York State Bar Association, in a statement. “The guidelines can help attorneys avoid possible perils of using AI, including inadvertently practicing law in a jurisdiction where they are not licensed or failing to notify clients or the courts of AI use.”

The committee also flagged familiar hazards, such as biased training data that may deepen existing inequities. Confidentiality is another concern: If an AI tool learns from one client’s information in a way that makes it available in another client’s matter, lawyers must turn to the New York Rules of Professional Conduct.

The report cautioned against building tools that deliver automated legal services in ways that could amount to unauthorized practice or using AI to pass as a human with prospective clients.

Supervising lawyers were reminded that they remain responsible for their subordinates’ compliance and should not assume that a law firm-approved tool or policy removes the need to review work on each matter.

According to Law360, the state bar association’s governing body adopted the report Saturday.

The fate of billable hours is in the hands of artificial intelligence

#7539. Court to consider federal inmate’s ability to use habeas to accelerate transfer to a halfway house or home confinement

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

In Maxwell v. Dinis, to be argued on Nov. 2, the Supreme Court will address a federal inmate’s ability to use a habeas statute, 28 U.S.C. § 2241, to contest the Federal Bureau of Prisons’ refusal to accelerate his transfer to a halfway house or home confinement.

By way of background, when the BOP designates a federal inmate spend time in a halfway house or in home confinement, that portion of the sentence is still considered part of the inmate’s term of imprisonment under federal law and, as such, is overseen by the BOP. That said, such a portion of a sentence is formally distinct from, for example, a term of federal supervised release, which begins after the term of imprisonment is completed and is overseen by a probation officer and a federal district court.

The special character of how a federal inmate serves a sentence in a halfway house or home confinement gives rise to the procedural question that the court is considering in Maxwell.

In 2007, William Maxwell conspired with members of the mob-related organized crime group, La Costa Nostra, to take over a Texas-based mortgage-loan company, FirstPlus Financial Group, Inc., and drain it of its assets. Specifically, Maxwell and others threatened the CEO of FirstPlus by saying that they would accuse him of bribery, money laundering, and other offenses, and took more than $14 million from the company, leaving it with less than $2,000 in its accounts. Convicted at trial in 2015 of numerous offenses, Maxwell was sentenced to 20 years in prison.

Maxwell did not have infractions while in prison, was moved to a low-security facility, and sought to accelerate his transfer to a halfway house or home confinement by participating in programs established by the First Step Act of 2018 under 18 U.S.C. § 3624(g)(1) and (2). Maxwell argued that the BOP failed to count some of these activities and that he was entitled to between 42 and 48 months of time credit that he did not receive. (Even under the BOP’s stricter calculations, according to the government Maxwell is eligible to be transferred to a halfway house on Jan. 22, 2027.)

The district court rejected Maxwell’s habeas petition, reasoning that he had failed to exhaust his administrative remedies. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit affirmed on the alternative ground that the circuit had adopted a bright-line rule that habeas relief under Section 2241 is unavailable unless the inmate’s claim would automatically entitle the inmate to accelerated release. According to the circuit court, since neither Maxwell’s requested relief of being transferred to a halfway house or home confinement “would entitle him to accelerated release,” he could not seek habeas relief.

What makes Maxwell’s situation tricky is that he is not attacking the validity of his conviction or sentence, which is what is contemplated by the federal habeas statute itself. And under the court’s precedent, it is at best unclear that a federal inmate can challenge conditions of his confinement, such as an inmate’s placement in solitary confinement or in a maximum-security facility. When state inmates have brought such claims about the conditions of confinement, the court has said that they must bring those claims in federal court under a civil rights statute, 42 U.S.C. § 1983, not via habeas.

But at least two initial points seem to weigh in Maxwell’s favor. First, in the 2023 case of Jones v. Hendrix, the court said that habeas remains available as a procedural mechanism for a federal prisoner to “challenge ‘the legality of his detention’ without attacking the validity of his sentence.” What Maxwell is trying to do (contest the BOP’s refusal to accelerate his transfer to a halfway house or home confinement) can plausibly be described as challenging the legality of his detention without challenging the lawfulness of his sentence. Second, and perhaps more importantly, in 1973, the court held in Preiser v. Rodriguez that a state prisoner must use a habeas petition – and not Section 1983 – to challenge the New York Department of Correctional Services’ denial of good-conduct time credits.

Maxwell begins his argument for why Section 2241 is available to him by relying on language tracing back to a concurring opinion by Justice Antonin Scalia. Specifically, in Skinner v. Switzer, the court stated that habeas relief is available for claims seeking to “reduce the prisoner’s level of custody” (quoting Scalia’s concurrence in Wilkinson v. Dotson). Maxwell also draws upon the language in Jones quoted above and the case of Preiser to argue that the situation in Preiser is a close analog to his circumstances and the court’s language in Jones leaves further room for challenges to the legality of an inmate’s detention.

Maxwell also points out that if habeas relief is unavailable, he has no other alternatives. The court has severely limited plaintiffs’ abilities to bring a civil-rights suit under Bivens v. Six Unknown Federal Narcotics Agents, for example, and a Section 1983 claim is inapplicable to suits against federal officials. The Administrative Procedures Act is also likely inapplicable because of a statute that limits review of the bureau of prisons’ decisions, as is injunctive relief through a suit in equity.

Notably, the government agrees with Maxwell that alternatives to habeas are unavailable. The government also declines to defend the lower court’s rule that habeas relief is limited to claims that automatically entitle the inmate to accelerated release. But the government endorses a narrower approach to when habeas relief is available than Maxwell. According to it, an inmate may seek habeas relief when arguing that his imprisonment has been unlawfully prolonged, a standard that does not require the inmate to show an entitlement to a sentence reduction. At the same time, the government’s standard would not extend to just any challenge to the “level of custody,” such as allowing an inmate’s classification in a maximum-security prison to be cognizable in habeas.

As for Maxwell, the government contends that his claim should be rejected for failure to exhaust all of his administrative remedies, the ground on which the district court dismissed the claim. On the “merits,” although the government says that Maxwell’s claim is of a type that may be brought in habeas, the government argues that, by statute, Congress has barred courts from reviewing the bureau of prisons’ classification of where an inmate “is placed during his term of imprisonment.” In the government’s view, this statute is fatal to Maxwell’s position.

Because the government declined to defend the court of appeals’ rule, the Supreme Court appointed a “friend of the court,” or amicus. The amicus contends that Maxwell’s and the government’s positions both create line-drawing problems. As to Maxwell’s position, the amicus argues that, given the wide continuum of conditions of incarceration that inmates face within the BOP’s system, determining whether a particular change in custody is meaningfully less restrictive would be difficult as a practical matter and require a fact-intensive, prisoner- and facility specific inquiry. As to the government’s position, the amicus argues that it has not offered any recognizable standard for deciding when an inmate’s imprisonment has been unlawfully prolonged.

In an effort to avoid those line-drawing problems, the amicus argues that habeas relief should instead be available in three relevant circumstances: (1) if the inmate’s claim implies that his physical detention must be shortened or terminated; (2) he is entitled to earlier release on bail or parole; or (3) the sentencing court ordered him to serve his sentence in a place it lacked jurisdiction to send him.

It is unclear whether the justices will find the amicus’ proposed circumstances appealing. But the amicus’s sustained attacks on the difficulties in applying Maxwell’s and the government’s position may well attract their interest.

Richard D. Cooke worked for the U.S. Department of Justice for 23 years, first at the Antitrust Division for 5 years and then as an Assistant United States Attorney in the Eastern District of Virginia for 18 years.

#7537. Wells Fargo faces labor board complaint over union vote

The National Labor Relations Board alleged the lender threatened and retaliated against workers in favor of unionization at a California branch.

The National Labor Relations Board has accused Wells Fargo of illegally threatening and retaliating against employees and coercing workers to prevent fair unionization votes at a California branch.

Most employees of an Atwater, California, branch who signed cards supporting unionization in December 2023 voted against unionization the following month, a regional director of the NLRB alleged, in a complaint filed Feb. 11 and seen by Bloomberg,

The NLRB claims Wells Fargo coerced workers to vote against unionization. Wells Fargo has denied that allegation.

The labor board wants the bank to recognize and negotiate with the union despite the vote, based on a 2023 precedent case. The 2023 Cemex ruling strengthened the NLRB's power to compel companies that violate labor laws to recognize unions.

However, Republicans and business groups oppose the precedent. The acting general counsel of NLRB, William Cowen, or his permanent replacement, could withdraw, amend, or settle the Wells Fargo complaint.

President Donald Trump appointed Cowen acting general counsel this month, days after firing NLRB’s previous chief lawyer Jennifer Abruzzo, a Biden appointee, and Democratic board member Gwynne Wilcox.

The email notifying Wilcox of her termination said she was being fired since she did not “share the objectives” of the present administration. Wilcox’s ouster has left the board with only two members coupled with existing vacancies and does not meet the minimum number of members needed to adjudicate routine cases.

Wilcox is suing Trump, alleging the president surpassed his authority in firing her and requesting that she be allowed to resume her work as an NLRB member.

The NLRB complaint does not signify a complete investigation or a full adjudication of the allegations; rather, the regional office found that the allegations may be sufficient to go to a hearing to consider all evidence and make credibility determinations, a Wells Fargo spokesperson noted.

Employees at the Atwater branch voted 3-1 to reject unionization in January 2024. The branch manager allegedly told staff she knew about organizing discussions and warned about camera surveillance. She also reportedly told workers that Wells Fargo would apply stricter work conditions and would make union supporters stay longer hours.

A Wells Fargo spokesperson said the bank trains its managers to respect the rights of its employees to freely associate and join or support a union, or to bargain collectively with a representative of their choosing.

“We train our managers to comply with labor law and respect the rights of our employees,” the spokesperson told Banking Dive via email. “In this case, the majority of eligible employees freely voted against a union in a Board supervised secret ballot election and the facts do not support allegations to the contrary.”

Wells Fargo is cooperating with the investigation but believes these allegations are unfounded and plans to defend the company and employees, the spokesperson added.

An NLRB hearing before a judge is scheduled for October, and Wells Fargo, if ordered to collectively bargain, can appeal to NLRB members in Washington, Bloomberg reported.

Recently, unionized Wells Fargo employees hit a new challenge in organizing. The bank's conduct management intake team won its union vote 21-16 in December, making it the first non-branch unit at Wells Fargo to unionize.

The team, which handles customer and employee complaints across various locations, has now filed an unfair labor practice charge with the NLRB through Wells Fargo Workers United-CWA. The complaint alleges that the bank illegally refuses to engage in collective bargaining following the certified union vote, American Banker reported. However, the bank contends it’s waiting for the outcome of the NLRB’s review and claims there were procedural flaws in the handling of the vote.

CWA unionized 24 Wells Fargo branches last year, with around 200 employees being organized.

Wells Fargo CEO Charlie Scharf pushed back on employee unionization efforts last April, saying it’s important to “make clear that we continue to believe that our employees are best served by working directly with Wells Fargo and our leadership team.”

#7533. The SEC has requested to delay climate rule arguments. What’s next?

Sustainable investing experts are not surprised by the delay and say it is expected to have minimal immediate impact.

Acting Securities and Exchange Commission Chair Mark Uyeda’s decision last week to ask the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals to delay arguments for the agency’s climate risk disclosure rule did not come as a surprise to regulatory experts in the space.

While the change is expected to have minimal immediate impact, it sets the stage for a shift in focus for the SEC under the Trump administration.

The SEC issued its long-awaited climate-risk disclosure rule last March, nearly two years after it was first proposed — and amid over 24,000 public comments. Uyeda was one of two commissioners to vote against the rule’s approval. The rule was immediately met with multiple lawsuits that were later consolidated into the Eighth Circuit. The spate of legal challenges led the agency to stay the rule’s implementation in April.

Given the agency’s stay and the change in administration, Tom Willman, regulatory lead for artificial intelligence sustainability platform Clarity AI, said Uyeda’s decision came “as no great surprise.”

“It is nevertheless disappointing that investors will be deprived of much-needed financially material information related to climate related risks,” Willman said by email Wednesday.

Julie Gorte, senior vice president of sustainable investing at Impax Asset Management was more blunt in an interview: “The only person on the planet who didn't see this coming was Rip Van Winkle,” she said Wednesday.

Uyeda’s recommended pullback on defending the SEC climate rule follows his prior critiques of the rule. During the hearing on the final climate rule, in the weeks after it was finalized and in his Feb. 11 statement announcing the delay request, Uyeda maintained his belief that the SEC does not have the authority to promulgate the rule or require such disclosures.

Jenner & Block Partner Jennifer Lee, a former assistant director of the SEC Enforcement Division, said Uyeda’s position is “consistent with the new, Republican-led SEC’s shift back to focusing on ‘bread and butter’ investor disclosure issues.” Lee, who now represents companies and financial institutions in regulatory investigations and litigation, told ESG Dive in emailed comments Thursday that she expects that focus to include an emphasis on materiality, while looking to avoid “overly prescriptive disclosure requirements for public companies.”

The change in SEC posture, however, is expected to have a minimal impact for companies or investors, according to Willman and Gorte.

“The impact of this is going to be extraordinarily minimal, partly because it was never enforced in the first place,” Gorte said Wednesday. “So we never had better climate reporting stimulated by U.S. regulatory postures to begin with. And for U.S. companies, or for any company really, a lot of the big ones are probably still going to have to be reporting on all the same things that were in that rule because of [other jurisdictions].”

Willman echoed that note and said that many U.S. companies already voluntarily report climate risks due to investor demand, in addition to growing regulatory requirements both overseas in jurisdictions like the European Union, and stateside in California. New York recently reintroduced its own version of California’s climate disclosure laws.

Additionally, Stephen O’Day, a partner at Smith, Gambrell & Russell, noted the intervenors in the case could continue the rule’s defense, even though the SEC’s announcement indicates this iteration of the agency is not inclined to defend the rules. In the case of the climate rule, 18 states and the District of Columbia have signed on as intervenors to support the agency’s rule.

O’Day said a similar process happened after intervenors continued the defense for enforcement actions taken by the Clinton-era administration for violations of the Clean Air Act by coal-fired plants. Ultimately, the intervenors prevailed, and the Supreme Court upheld the actions.

“The proceedings pending in the Eighth Circuit involve challenges filed by multiple parties and intervenors, any of which could seek to continue defense of the SEC rules,” O’Day said. “So, while the court may grant the requested 45-day pause, it remains to be seen whether any such pause will result in the end of the SEC’s final rules.”

Regardless, sustainability programs and disclosures are expected to continue.

“Regulatory shifts don’t change the fundamental reality: physical climate risk is already priced into markets,” Lukky Ahmed, CEO of climate risk data and analytics platform Climate X, said by email Wednesday. Firms have a fiduciary responsibility to continue to assess, manage and disclose climate risks to their operations, Ahmed said.

“Integrating climate resilience and adaptation strategies isn’t just prudent — it’s essential for maintaining business performance, driving shareholder returns, and protecting communities," Ahmed said.

Despite the shifting federal policy stance, “there is a lot of faith that the drivers of sustainability remain in place no matter who is in anyone's White House,” Gorte told ESG Dive.

“If we don't solve the climate crisis, there are going to be … parts of the globe that are probably uninhabitable, or where people can't work outdoors in the summer. If we don't solve the biodiversity crisis, the prospects are even worse.” Gorte said. “So there are things that we have to do in order to preserve what we think of as life as we know it, and those drivers are going to remain in place.”

#7532. The Supreme Court and what constitutes cruel and unusual punishment

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

Earlier this month, the concept of cruel and unusual punishment briefly captured the country’s attention after the state of Tennessee on Sept. 30 tried and failed to execute Christa Pike. Pike, who was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of Colleen Slemmer, survived being injected with two lethal doses of pentobarbital. As she recovered from her injuries, including arm burns, at a Nashville hospital, commentators debated whether it would be cruel and unusual – and therefore unconstitutional – for Tennessee officials to seek to execute Pike again.

This debate drew attention to a range of past Supreme Court rulings on the death penalty, including a case in which the court allowed a second attempt at executing someone who, as a result of a mechanical problem, survived electrocution. However, it also highlighted a number of unresolved issues in this area, including how the constitutional analysis may change if a state is found to have ignored warnings that an execution attempt may go awry.

Kelsey Dallas is SCOTUSblog's managing editor and the primary author of the SCOTUStoday newsletter.

#7530. Former judge accused of shooting gun toward unwanted trick-or-treaters

Former Oklahoma Judge Jerry Herberger was arrested recently after allegedly shooting a gun toward unwanted trick-or-treaters. (Photo from the Stephens County Sheriff’s Office)

A former Oklahoma judge was arrested recently after allegedly shooting a gun toward unwanted trick-or-treaters who came near his home on Halloween.

Former Judge Jerry Herberger, 73, of Duncan, Oklahoma, was booked in the Stephens County Jail in Oklahoma for assault and battery with a deadly weapon, attempted murder and possession of a firearm while intoxicated, the Lawton Constitution reports.

Police were called Saturday night after witnesses said an intoxicated Herberger had threatened trick-or-treaters if they came to his home. With a gun in his hand, he allegedly fired off a round in the children’s direction, according to the Lawton Constitution.

As officers prepared to make contact at the home, Herberger allegedly pointed a gun at one of the officers, said Loisdawn Jones, the director of communications for the city of Duncan, Oklahoma. He then complied with officers’ commands and exited the residence, where he was taken into custody and booked into the Stephens County Jail.

#7527. Court to hear argument in religious discrimination challenge brought by Catholic preschools in Colorado

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Supreme Court will hear oral argument on Nov. 3 in a challenge brought by Catholic preschools in Colorado, which argue that their exclusion from Colorado’s universal preschool program is a form of religious discrimination in violation of the First Amendment, because Colorado will not provide them with an exemption from rules that would require them to admit everyone – including LGBTQ children and children with LGBTQ parents.

The Catholic preschools say that they “have no objection to Colorado’s decision to allow over 1,000 … preschools to selectively serve the communities they are designed to serve.” Instead, the preschools emphasize, they “simply want the same accommodation extended to them.”

Colorado counters that the Catholic preschools “remain welcome to participate in” the universal preschool program. However, the state writes, if they do, they must be “subject to the same equal-opportunity requirements that apply to all other publicly funded preschools—public and private, secular and religious.”

Under the universal preschool program, families in Colorado can receive up to 15 hours of free preschool per week at participating schools. To be part of the program, preschools must meet state standards in areas such as employee training; they are also required to sign a nondiscrimination agreement, in which they consent to “provide eligible children an equal opportunity to enroll and receive preschool services regardless of race, ethnicity, religious affiliation, sexual orientation, gender identity, lack of housing, income level, or disability.” Colorado does not allow them to refuse to serve LGBTQ families, because it believes such refusals would violate the nondiscrimination agreement.

The plaintiffs in the case are the Archdiocese of Denver, two Catholic parishes with preschools (one of which has since closed), and two parents of preschool-aged children. They went to federal court to challenge the state’s policy, arguing that making Catholic preschools’ participation in the universal preschool program contingent on accepting the agreement amounts to unlawful religious discrimination and that the First Amendment requires Colorado to create a religious exemption to allow them to participate in the program.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit ruled for the state. It acknowledged that in a line of decisions, the Supreme Court has held that “when a state offers subsidies for private education, it cannot categorically withhold those funds from religious institutions.” In the 10th Circuit’s view, however, those cases do not apply to the preschools’ challenge because Colorado “did not exclude” religious preschools from the universal preschool program. To the contrary, the court of appeals wrote, it “welcomed and actively solicited their participation” and it is not seeking “to prohibit funds from being used for religious purposes.” “The restrictions imposed by the nondiscrimination requirement universally cover enrollment policies and conduct, but they are not a targeted burden on religious use.”

The court of appeals also rejected the challengers’ contention that the nondiscrimination requirement is unconstitutional because it burdens their right to freely exercise their religious beliefs. In the court’s view, Colorado’s conditions were neutral and generally applied to every preschool, regardless of religion – the kind of government actions, the Supreme Court held in 1990 in Employment Division v. Smith, that normally do not violate the Constitution.

Although a regulation issued by the Colorado Department of Early Childhood contains a series of preferences to facilitate the matching of families to preschools, including a “catchall” preference that allows preschools to request (and the state to grant) a preference not listed in the regulation, the court of appeals said that preference is not the kind of individualized exemption that would render the law not generally applicable, because the preschools are still required to comply with the nondiscrimination requirement.

The court of appeals also rebuffed the challengers’ argument that the nondiscrimination requirement is not generally applicable because the program permits schools to give preferences to low-income families and children with disabilities. As an initial matter, the court of appeals suggested, it was “not persuaded” that such preferences actually are exceptions to the nondiscrimination requirement because they were intended to protect such children and families and do not discriminate against wealthier families or children without disabilities. But in any event, it continued, the nondiscrimination agreement is still generally applicable because the Supreme Court’s cases only prohibit the state from treating religious activity less favorably than comparable secular activity. And the preferences for low-income families and children with disabilities are not comparable, the court of appeals concluded, because – unlike the exemption that the challengers in this case seek – they do not “undermine[] the government’s asserted interest in ensuring equal access to preschools.”

The challengers came to the Supreme Court in November 2025, asking the justices to weigh in – which they agreed in April 2026 to do.

At the Supreme Court, the justices will review two main questions. The first is the scope of the court’s 2022 decision in Carson v. Makin, in which the court struck down a Maine law that allowed public funding to be used for private schools, but not for schools that provide religious instruction.

The challengers contend that under Carson, this case should be “an uncomplicated one.” Colorado, the challengers say, “knowingly excluded Catholic preschools solely on account of their religious exercise” – specifically, “their religious practices of ensuring that all enrolling families are supportive of the Catholic Church’s teachings on sex and marriage and of treating enrolled four-year-olds in accordance with their biological sex.” That exclusion, the challengers argue, places a burden on their ability to exercise their religion, in violation of the Constitution.

Colorado counters that Carson “applied the settled principle that government may not target religion for disfavored treatment.” What the preschools are seeking instead, it says, is a “new rule that would trigger strict scrutiny whenever public-benefits conditions incidentally burden religiously motivated conduct.”

The second question before the justices centers on what a challenger has to show to prevail on a claim that a law is not generally applicable for purposes of Smith.

In Tandon v. Newsom, the challengers contend, the Supreme Court made clear that, for purposes of Smith, “[a] law is not generally applicable if it ‘treat[s] any comparable secular activity more favorably than religious exercise’” – a test that the universal preschool program fails. Colorado created the universal-preschool program to ensure equal access for all preschool-aged children, they emphasize. Because the exemptions for low-income families and children with disabilities allow preschools “to provide families with unequal access based on protected characteristics,” the challengers argue, “they undermine Colorado’s asserted interest in equal access ‘in a similar way’ to” the religious accommodation that the challengers seek. Moreover, the challengers add, the program also fails the “general applicability” test under Smith because it gives Colorado discretion, through the preference system, to allow participating preschools “to discriminate in favor of LGBTQ families and other groups,” such as “‘gender-nonconforming children,’ ‘children of color,’ or members of ‘the LGBTQ community.’”

Colorado pushes back, telling the justices that the law creating the universal preschool program “expressly prioritizes specialized services for” children from low-income families and children with disabilities, based on the state’s “longstanding awareness that ensuring equal opportunity for these children often requires providing them with additional support.” But “allowing publicly funded preschools to provide” such services does not “allow any secular conduct that undermines Colorado’s equal-opportunity interests”; therefore, it says, the law is generally applicable for purposes of Smith.

Similarly, Colorado continues, the system of preferences, used to match preschools with families, that are “unrelated to the characteristics protected by the equal-opportunity requirements, by definition, are not exceptions from those requirements.” It is clear, the state stressed, that such preferences can be implemented “only when” they “do not violate the equal-opportunity requirements.”

Correction (Oct. 30 at 11:40 a.m.): A prior version of this article stated that “a participating faith-based preschool may prioritize the enrollment of families that belong to the same faith as that school.”

Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

#7526. DEI attacks are likely to refine and improve programs, experts say

The intense pressure to end diversity initiatives has led companies to scrutinize their policies. Many of the attacks will end up strengthening DEI programs.

The politicians, provocateurs and think tanks that in the past few years have worked to dismantle diversity, equity and inclusion may not appreciate the full consequences of their efforts.

They’ve used a variety of tactics, in the public and private sectors, including White House executive orders; lawsuits or the threat of lawsuits; shareholder proposals; and needling on social media. They’ve notched high-profile wins, most notably the Supreme Court’s ruling against affirmative action and capitulation at several companies, including retailers and brands that have ended or scaled back their DEI programs.

The successful challenges, inevitably, are forcing scrutiny of DEI practices. But they also provide an opportunity to reinforce DEI goals and execution, which David Glasgow, executive director of New York University’s Meltzer Center for Diversity, Inclusion, and Belonging, sees as a silver lining.

Indeed, the victories are hardly universal. Because diversity, equity and inclusion are good for business for a variety of reasons, most companies are not abandoning DEI. So far in 2025, Target, Nike and Costco are among those that have defended at least some aspects of their policies (in Costco’s case, vociferously). As the Heritage Foundation, a major DEI foe, noted in November, most Fortune 500 companies continue to publicly commit to DEI.

“It is a time for companies to refine and strengthen their inclusion efforts in ways that reduce the risk in the short term — because the risk is real, and we know that — and in ways that are sustainable in the long term,” said Adrienne Pulido, vice president of inclusion insights at Kantar. “So it is looking at both ends of the spectrum, in terms of being very clear about what inclusion means to their business.”

DEI is being pilloried as discriminatory and unfair, yet these systems are designed to create a business that is neither. That is, a business where employees have a variety of backgrounds and perspectives (diversity); hiring, promotion and other actions are executed fairly (equity); and the culture is comfortable and inviting to all who work there (inclusion).

“Unpacking what DEI is and what inclusion is, is part of this moment we're in and part of the conversation that companies need to have about their strategies,” Pulido said by video conference. “What does DEI mean to the business itself? What does it mean to the business and to the future business? Because the demographics of the country are changing, and our research shows that inclusion as a concept, as an idea, is very popular among Americans of all backgrounds.”

DEI goals for most companies are more important than ever because the markets for their products and services are more diverse than they were a decade or more ago, according to Effenus Henderson, who has worked in recruiting, staffing and succession planning at companies in the U.S. and abroad since the 1970s.

“This attack is amplified through the use of social media and technology and psychometrics, where emotions get aroused and reinforced,” he said by phone. “But fundamental to all this is that DEI is not about creating systems that are discriminatory, or about quotas, or a focus on one thing at the exclusion of others. I don't think organizations have really done that. What they have been doing is really trying to expand participation because of the growing demographic change that we're seeing.”

The need to develop DEI strategies that fit with and further business strategies dictates the involvement of leadership, according to Henderson. Too often, though, they are left to the human resources department, leaving companies at risk of adopting DEI programming that is ineffective and possibly indefensible.

“The companies that are able to navigate this generally are the ones where leadership has spent the time talking about it,” he said. “It's not just about reacting to the George Floyd situation or to civil rights laws or litigation. It's really, ‘How do we integrate this as a part of the DNA of who we are as an organization?’ If your organization is more performative, then they don't really understand how it helps to shape business strategy and policy.”

DEI should be treated like any other strategic priority, according to Tim Heneveld, country director for Pergolux in North America. With DEI under the spotlight, it’s a good moment to reassess whether hiring, workplace environment, leadership and operational strategies fit with broader aims.

“That means setting measurable goals, using data to track impact, and holding leadership accountable,” Heneveld said by email. “Some organizations are feeling pressure to scale back DEI, but I think doing so would be shortsighted. Instead, companies should refine their DEI strategies, aligning them with long-term business goals rather than reacting to what they are seeing in the media or any other outside factors. I've experienced, firsthand, workplaces can attract top talent, strengthen their teams, and improve retention.”

In some cases, companies are continuing with their DEI efforts, but changing the names of their initiatives or titles of their employees, experts said.

Crafting DEI initiatives and training is always a work in progress because businesses, markets and demographics evolve, according to Henderson. For many companies, that may mean avoiding those three letters of the alphabet, or the words “diversity, equity and inclusion.” But that, too, requires some thought, he said.

“Is continuing to refer to it under those banners still appropriate, and if I look at renaming it, am I doing that to help enhance our appeal to the markets of the customers and employees we serve? Are we doing it as a reactive, defensive thing for a short-term issue that's hot and heavy right now?” he said. “Get clarity around your objectives, the alignment with your strategies, and then decide whether how you are framing it today will work for you tomorrow and the day after. At some companies, it may mean one thing, and to others it may mean something else.”

The list of lawsuits against DEI programs tracked by the Meltzer Center is long, and getting longer.

Most of these claims invoke civil rights laws intended to end or prevent unfair hiring practices or contracts. Frequently that includes Title VII of the Civil Rights Act, barring discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex and national origin; Section 1981 of the federal code barring discrimination in contracts; and the U.S. Constitution’s equal protection clause, according to Glasgow. The Meltzer Center advises companies to avoid DEI practices that give preference to members of certain groups and involve a tangible benefit.

Evaluating whether a company’s DEI programs run afoul of the latest interpretations of these codes entails enlisting attorneys or other compliance experts.

“This has become a thriving legal practice area,” Glasgow said.

Any business strategy should always be grounded in risk mitigation, and this is just another place for companies to check, according to Henderson. Companies may learn that, to avoid risk, certain aspects of their DEI programs should change.

Others may find that they pass muster. In its proxy statement urging shareholders to vote against a proposal that could have weakened its DEI programs, Costco’s board of directors made clear that the retailer regularly evaluates its “practices concerning compliance with law, including evolving Supreme Court decisions.”

In describing how Costco obeys the law and does not discriminate in hiring, promotion and other practices, the board also provided a litany of protected statuses. This is a reminder that, while civil rights statutes are being leveraged to overturn DEI practices, they nevertheless do bar discrimination for a host of reasons. Moreover, any company that does business abroad will encounter antidiscrimination law that isn’t being disrupted by political activism the way it is in the U.S., Henderson said.

“If you look at Canada, Europe, Asia and South America, there are regulations and laws that support and value diversity,” he said. “So backing away from DEI may, in fact, create harm for your business strategies in other parts of the world. It's not a simple answer, and it just depends on who you are.”

While it may seem like DEI programs are quickly getting scrapped in order to avoid controversy, most are simply under review, Glasgow and others said.

“I think it's prompting a much deeper reflection within companies, not just on what is strictly legal or illegal in what we're doing, but on what has been working and what has not been working,” Glasgow said. “Could we be doing this work more effectively, in a way that actually helps us achieve our business goals, or helps us create the kind of culture that we want to create? Are there things that have been low impact, or maybe even have a negative impact, that we should get rid of, even if it's not for legal reasons? I think the moment that we're living in now could be a helpful reset moment for the field.”

#7524. Groups ask Supreme Court to leave lower court order in place halting border wall construction in southwestern Texas

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The plaintiffs challenging the Trump administration’s efforts to build a border wall in the Big Bend region of southwestern Texas urged the Supreme Court on Thursday to leave in place an order by a federal trial judge in El Paso temporarily halting the construction. Eric Glitzenstein, a lawyer representing the plaintiffs, told the justices in a 40-page filing that granting the federal government’s request to lift that order would allow the Trump administration to “immediately resume blasting, bulldozing, road construction, and other border barrier-related construction across one of the most remote and ecologically and culturally significant landscapes in the United States.”

The dispute centers on three waivers of various environmental and conservation laws that then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and her successor, Markwayne Mullin, issued earlier this year to authorize construction of the border wall in the Big Bend region, including areas in Big Bend National Park. Noem and Mullin relied on a provision of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996 that gives the Secretary of Homeland Security the power to “waive all legal requirements” necessary “to ensure expeditious construction” of border walls and roads. With the waivers, Noem and Mullin determined that additional border barriers are required in the Big Bend area because it “is an area of high illegal entry.”

The plaintiffs in this case – an environmental group, a local landowner, and a group formed to preserve a church – went to federal court to challenge the waivers’ legality. On Oct. 2, U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone temporarily barred the Department of Homeland Security from continuing construction on the border wall in the Big Bend region “until and unless” the government complies with environmental and other applicable laws.

In a written opinion issued on Oct. 14 to explain her reasoning, Cardone concluded that the challengers were likely to prevail on their claim that under the major questions doctrine – the idea that if Congress intends to give a federal agency the power to make decisions of vast economic or political significance, it must say so explicitly – the DHS secretary did not have the authority to issue the waivers.

As an initial matter, Cardone rejected the government’s contention that she did not have the power to consider the challengers’ claims because they arose from a statute, while IIRIRA only allows federal courts to hear challenges to waiver decisions if they involve the Constitution. The major questions doctrine, she said, is a “constitutional … rule” based on the idea that “courts should expect Congress to speak clearly when it delegates major lawmaking authority to the executive.”

Turning to the question of whether the major questions doctrine barred the waivers, she observed that both the government and the challengers “appear to agree that the waiver of all legal requirements to construct a border wall in the Big Bend Sector is of ‘major economic and political significance.’” The key issue, she continued, is thus whether Congress clearly gave the DHS secretary the power to issue the Big Bend waivers. It did not, she wrote. She emphasized that another provision of IIRIRA authorizes the DHS secretary to “take such actions as may be necessary to install additional physical barriers and roads … in the vicinity of the United States border to deter illegal crossings in areas of high illegal entry into the United States.” When that provision is read together with the waiver provision, she said, it means that the DHS secretary can only waive legal requirements for “construction ‘to deter illegal crossings in areas of high illegal entry.’”

But the Big Bend region is not, she contended, such an area: although it “comprises over 25% of the U.S.-Mexico border,” it accounts for only a tiny percentage (“between 0.3% and 2.2%”) of all of the people apprehended crossing the border. This means, she said, that “if the Big Bend Sector is an area of high illegal entry, so is every other sector, and the waiver authority would apply to the entire U.S.-Mexico border. If that were the case, Congress could have simply authorized construction ‘to deter illegal crossings.’” The major questions doctrine instructs courts to avoid “interpretations that would render limiting language meaningless,” Cardone concluded.

The Trump administration came to the Supreme Court on Oct. 21, asking the justices to pause Cardone’s order and to grant review and summarily reverse it. First, U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer argued, the district court did not have the power to consider the challengers’ claim based on the major questions doctrine because their complaint specifically alleged that the DHS secretary “lacked ‘clear congressional authorization’ … to issue the waivers” under the IIRIRA – a statutory claim that “Congress denied district courts” the authority “to entertain.” But in any event, Sauer continued, “[e]ven assuming that the Secretary’s waiver authority implicates a question of ‘vast economic and political significance,’ Congress did clearly authorize the Secretary both to build border barriers and to waive legal requirements in order to facilitate their expeditious construction.”

In their brief on Thursday, the challengers insisted that the major questions doctrine applied to their claim, stressing that “the decision to waive myriad federal, state, local, and tribal laws across vast geography for the purpose of building border infrastructure, even through national and state parks where border crossings are miniscule, is a truly ‘extraordinary’ assertion of power.” “Whatever authority Congress delegated, it did not clearly authorize the sweeping exercise of power asserted here, and” the government’s “actions therefore amount to a constitutional violation of the major questions doctrine.”

The challengers also argued that DHS will not suffer any permanent harm if the construction is temporarily blocked – one of the factors that courts consider in deciding whether to award temporary relief. To the contrary, they noted, before Cardone issued her order halting construction, “in response to intense local opposition,” DHS “voluntarily paused construction for weeks in vast portions of the project area.”

Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

#7522. Kim Kardashian aims to retake bar exam

Reality TV star Kim Kardashian speaks onstage during the 2020 Winter TCA Tour on Jan. 18, 2020, in Pasadena, California. (Photo by David Livingston/Getty Images)

Reality TV star Kim Kardashian still holds ambitions to become a lawyer and plans to retake the bar exam—someday.

Kardashian, who failed the California bar exam in 2025, said she is “always thinking about the bar” and is “still all in,” she told People on Monday. “I’m going to take my time and wait until the moment is right, when I have some free time to focus on it.”

Kardashian, who plays a lawyer on Hulu’s legal drama All’s Fair, was among the 7,362 candidates who completed the July 2025 administration of the California bar, according to the State Bar of California.

The state’s test is considered one of the most difficult in the country, and only 54.8% passed last year and 48.3% in July, according to the state bar.

Kardashian did not attend law school and does not have an undergraduate degree. She has followed the state’s alternative pathway that allows candidates to take the bar exam by learning the law through apprenticeship and study.

California is one of the few states that allow lawyers to become lawyers by “reading the law.”

#7521. Judge halts CFPB firings

In the same order, the bureau was told not to delete any agency data or transfer its reserve funding to the Fed or anywhere else. The CFPB then reportedly placed most workers on administrative leave.

A federal judge has ordered the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and its acting director, Russ Vought, not to terminate any agency employee except for cause related to job performance or conduct until March 3, when another hearing in the case will take place.

The bureau responded, however, by placing on administrative leave all employees except those asked to return to work by “the Acting Director, Chief Legal Officer, or another designee,” according to an email from the CFPB’s human capital operations manager that was seen by Bloomberg Law.

The court order on Friday came after the National Treasury Employees Union urged Judge Amy Berman Jackson on Thursday to block Vought from a “mass firing” it believed would affect 95% of the bureau’s workforce as early as Friday.

In the same Friday order, Berman Jackson demanded that the CFPB “not delete, destroy, remove, or impair” any data or agency records covered by the Federal Records Act.

Berman Jackson also ordered the CFPB and Vought not to transfer money from the bureau's reserve funds, other than "to satisfy” the agency’s “ordinary operating obligations.” That includes returning money from the CFPB’s reserve funds to the Federal Reserve, as Vought said this month he would do.

The data-related developments follow a declaration the CFPB’s former chief technologist, Erie Meyer, filed with the court Friday, warning that databases holding 12 years’ worth of information the agency has collected would soon be deleted and “irretrievably lost.”

Affected data would include “supervisory and examination records of financial institutions, enforcement action data, consumer complaints, personal consumer information, and market research records,” Meyer wrote.

Loss of data that tracks institutions’ financial behavior “would impair the Bureau's ability to identify risks and respond to emerging threats within the financial system,” Meyer wrote.

“This could destabilize markets, allow bad actors to exploit weaknesses in financial institutions, and undermine public trust in the financial system,” she wrote.

It would also open the financial system to market manipulation, Meyer asserted.

“Tech companies moving into financial services could gain an illegal competitive advantage by accessing sensitive consumer financial data or enforcement records, and the audit logs of that activity could be deleted,” she wrote. “This could result in unfair competition and undermine market integrity.”

That may serve as a reference to X Money, the payments tool set for launch this year in a partnership between card network Visa and social media platform X, owned by Trump adviser Elon Musk, who’s also seen as the architect behind the Department of Government Efficiency, which infiltrated the CFPB this month.

The deletion of CFPB data “would leave consumers without critical recourse in the event of financial harm caused by institutions under the Bureau's jurisdiction,” Meyer wrote. Further, she asserted, it would make the CFPB’s Consumer Response database “unavailable and/or unreliable, severely hamper — if not entirely take down — the Bureau’s website, and likely result in the loss of mandatory public reporting the Bureau has previously done.”

Friday’s order may represent a relief to CFPB employees, but it doesn’t apply to bureau employees who have already been terminated. The agency last Tuesday terminated roughly 70 probationary employees, then Thursday fired another 70 to 100 term employees – those whose contracts have set limits between one and four years.

Altogether, last week’s firings cut roughly 10% of the CFPB's workforce, according to American Banker.

The CFPB was not the only banking regulator to see workforce reductions last week. Roughly 500 employees at the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp., or about 8% of its workforce, accepted a deferred resignation offer from the Trump administration, Bloomberg Law reported Friday, citing a spokesperson for the agency.

The FDIC then terminated probationary employees, the outlet reported Monday, though the number of employees affected remained unclear.

An FDIC spokesperson on Friday did not detail how deeply certain units of the regulator were affected.

A lawyer representing the CFPB workers’ union laid out the urgency of Friday’s court action.

”I’m asking that they don't fire the entire agency tonight,” Deepak Gupta, a founding principal at Gupta Wessler, told the court, according to American Banker. “I don’t want to leave the courthouse without some assurance that the mass layoff is not going to happen and then become a fait accompli.”

The workers’ union asked Thursday for a temporary restraining order to stop the firings, but agreed to seek a preliminary injunction instead.

That mirrors a case in the U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland, in which the city of Baltimore sued the CFPB, claiming Vought’s move to return the agency’s funding to the Fed would effectively shut down the bureau “by fiat.”

The government agreed Thursday that Vought would refrain from transferring money out of the CFPB’s reserve fund or returning money to the Fed or Treasury until Feb. 28, or upon a “contrary order” from the court, Bloomberg Law reported.

Still, in the workers’ union case, Brad Rosenberg, a Justice Department special counsel, objected to the request for a preliminary injunction.

"We don't think any preliminary relief is appropriate at this stage because we don't think the plaintiffs are likely to succeed on the merits," he said, according to American Banker.

Among the employees the CFPB terminated Thursday is Julia Barnard, who served as the agency’s student loan ombudsman since last February. Her position is mandated by the 2010 Dodd-Frank Act.

“This work matters,” Barnard said in a statement issued by the Student Borrower Protection Center. “It’s a lifeline for borrowers and a safeguard against a system that too often fails them. Dismantling this function is unconscionable and will cost real people real money.”

Delaying any further moves to slash the CFPB workforce would at least give employees time to plan and budget for their personal futures. Employees of the agency are entitled by law to 60 days’ notice of job loss. But last week’s firings came with no notice and with immediate effect.

Further, terminations for cause (probationary employees, for example, were notified that they were deemed “not fit for continued employment because [their] ability, knowledge and skills do not fit the Agency’s current needs”) left those employees without access to severance, one lawyer with the CFPB told ABC News.

In Vought’s first week as the CFPB’s acting director, the bureau’s headquarters were closed to employees, who were ordered to stop all bureau work. A tip line was also set up for people to report on employees who might be conducting work.
