Three legal experts Nieman Lab consulted were skeptical about the revised terms of service and Meta’s most recent statements. “[The update] doesn’t address my concerns,” said James Grimmelmann, a professor of digital and information law at Cornell Law School. “While it adds more language about the permitted uses, [the] ‘develop…advertising and business products’ [language] is still broad enough to drive a truck through. This does nothing to restrict the ‘associated with your products or services’ [language] that would let Meta scrape entire sites.” University of Wisconsin law professor Benjamin Sobel explained that robots.txt indicates a website’s preferences, but compliance with those is completely voluntary. He likened it to a homeowner putting up a sign saying, “Don’t look at my house.” Putting up that sign doesn’t give the homeowner an enforceable legal right to stop people from looking at the house. “You can still express the preference, and unless it’s a legally enforceable preference, it can still be ignored all the same,” he said. “We’ve heard you and want to clarify: the crawling terms we consolidated only applied to our ads and business products, and we’ve clarified that in the terms themselves,” a spokesperson said in a statement, claiming publishers can still update their scraping preferences using robots.txt files. “This is not about scraping news sites, and these updates don’t give us new rights that supersede those preferences.”

Meta’s current terms permit it to scrape websites associated with business accounts, but only in a very specific scenario. That language is found in its terms of service for when accounts use Meta’s generative AI features to run advertisements. The scraped content can only be used to “optimize your ads.”

A Meta spokesperson said the company is incorporating its “Ad Creative Generative AI Terms” into its general commercial terms to make them easier to understand.

Three legal experts Nieman Lab consulted were skeptical about the revised terms of service and Meta’s most recent statements.

“[The update] doesn’t address my concerns,” said James Grimmelmann, a professor of digital and information law at Cornell Law School. “While it adds more language about the permitted uses, [the] ‘develop…advertising and business products’ [language] is still broad enough to drive a truck through. This does nothing to restrict the ‘associated with your products or services’ [language] that would let Meta scrape entire sites.”

University of Wisconsin law professor Benjamin Sobel explained that robots.txt indicates a website’s preferences, but compliance with those is completely voluntary. He likened it to a homeowner putting up a sign saying, “Don’t look at my house.” Putting up that sign doesn’t give the homeowner an enforceable legal right to stop people from looking at the house.

“You can still express the preference, and unless it’s a legally enforceable preference, it can still be ignored all the same,” he said.

Prior to the update on Friday, the European Publishers Council announced that it would formally petition the E.U.’s telecommunications regulatory authorities and its executive body, the European Commission, to “scrutinize these terms urgently, including their implications for copyright, contractual fairness and abuse of market power.”

The United Kingdom News Media Association, the trade organization representing British media, issued a statement on Friday calling for government officials to intervene.

“This shameless landgrab attempt from Meta to scrape anything and everything from news publishers and business websites to train their AI products is the worst kind of arrogant tech platform bullying,” said chief executive Theo Bamber. “We urgently need Ministers and regulators to stand up for British creators and the business community by calling out this outrageous behaviour and preventing Meta from setting this dreadful precedent.”

The News/Media Alliance — the largest news publishing trade association in the United States — denounced the terms, with president and CEO Danielle Coffey calling the update “outrageous and probably illegal.”

“The company’s decision to withhold access to its audience unless businesses allow Meta to scrape content from their websites is an appalling, bad-faith policy, and a clear abuse of the company’s market power,” Coffey said. “It cannot be allowed to be implemented on October 30.”

This story has been updated to include comments from Meta.

#7429. Druski is one of Netflix’s biggest creator signings. What can he do with a multi-year deal?

Druski is coming to Netflix. On December 1, the ascendant creator (whose real name is Drew Desbordes) will premiere Collect & Praise, a comedy series that spoofs the culture of megachurches.

Since making a name for himself with Instagram Live broadcasts and short-form sketches, Druski has become a bankable star. He has appeared in campaigns alongside traditional celebs, spun podcast gold, and even launched his own agency.

His fame will reach new heights (and new audiences) on November 7. That’s when he will become the first social media creator to host Saturday Night Live.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Druski leveraged his expanding network to make Collect & Praise a reality. The self-funded series, produced through his company 4LIFERS Entertainment, builds on viral sketches he has posted and co-stars veteran comic actor Mike Epps. On the Diary of a CEO podcast, Druski told Steven Bartlett that his show triggered a “bidding war,” with Netflifx coming out on top.

As we’ve seen with the streaming platform’s other creator deals, its agreement with Druski will go beyond original content. Netflix will license content from the creator’s back catalog, including his dating show parody Coulda Been Love and his semi-serious label Coulda Been Records.

“I’ve built my platform by creating characters and comedy that resonate with people,” Druski said in a statement. “This partnership with Netflix will give me the resources to build on that comedy foundation and bring my work to a new global audience. It’s a tremendous opportunity for our team at 4LIFERS Entertainment to expand our reach, develop original programming for the masses and take our creativity to new heights.”

A multi-year agreement will give Druski plenty of time to flex his creative muscles. Netflix’s press release promises “future Druski projects” on the platform; those ventures will be announced at a later date.

Netflix certainly hasn’t been shy about signing creators. It has inked deals with Mark Rober, Alan Chikin Chow, and several other digital standouts as it looks to encroach on YouTube’s territory.

That spending spree, however, hasn’t been able to abate the negative headlines at Netflix HQ. A big round of layoffs hit last month, and erratic earnings have sent the streamer’s stock price tumbling. Co-CEO Ted Sarandos, normally an optimist about his company’s outlook, has admitted that Netflix “could do better.”

Perhaps Druski’s star power will be the shot in the arm Netflix needs to set itself on an upward course. If, however, Collect & Praise doesn’t pan out as expected, Netflix may be left wondering what coulda been.
